title: World Religions: The Big Picture
objective: After this level you can name the world's major religious traditions and the few things nearly all of them share: beliefs, practices, community and sacred stories.
summary: Christianity and Islam are the largest religions, then Hinduism and Buddhism, with Judaism and many smaller faiths besides. Nearly all share beliefs, practices, a community and sacred stories.

cards.headline: Most people on Earth belong to a religion. What do they all share?
cards.body: Religions can look wildly different from the outside: different prayers, foods, festivals and holy places. Before we meet them one by one, here is the quick tour, and the few things nearly all of them have in common.

cards.headline: The big names
cards.body: Christianity is the world's largest religion, and Islam is second. Among religions, Hinduism and Buddhism come next. Judaism is much smaller, about 15 million people. Then come Sikhs, Jains, Baha'is, Daoists, Shintoists, Zoroastrians and many smaller communities. And one of the biggest groups on the map isn't a religion at all: people who don't identify with any. This course visits all of them, in their own words.

cards.headline: So what is a religion?
cards.body: One major encyclopedia puts it this way: religion is people's relation to what they regard as holy, sacred, spiritual or divine. Notice the word regard. The definition describes what people hold sacred; it doesn't rule on it. And religion is more than ideas in someone's head. The same encyclopedia lists worship, moral conduct, right belief and taking part in a religious community as parts of religious life.

mascot.line: Keep these four in your pocket. In Level 3 a scholar turns them into seven, and they'll fit any faith you meet.

cards.headline: Four things nearly every faith has
cards.body: Look closely and nearly every tradition shows the same four things. Beliefs about what matters most. Practices, from worship to right conduct. A community: the scholar Ninian Smart noted that every religious movement lives in a group of people, often organized as a Church, a Sangha or an umma. And sacred stories. Every faith, Smart wrote, hands down vital stories: of creation, of great founders and saints, of what will come at the end of time.

Religion is people's relation to what they hold sacred
Nearly every faith has beliefs, practices, community and sacred stories

title: What Counts as a Religion?
objective: After this level you can explain why scholars struggle to define religion, comparing a definition by belief in spiritual beings with one by what religion does for a community.
summary: Tylor defined religion by belief in spiritual beings; Durkheim by practices that unite a moral community. Each fits some traditions awkwardly, and in East Asia the word itself is new.

cards.headline: Try defining religion in one sentence. Scholars have argued since the 1870s.
cards.body: Every definition seems to leave someone out, or let too much in. Here are the two classic attempts, and why the problem runs deeper than wording.

cards.headline: Definition one: what people believe
cards.body: In 1871 the anthropologist Edward Tylor offered a minimum definition: religion is belief in spiritual beings. Scholars call this kind of definition substantive, because it names the content: spirits, gods or other unseen realities. It's short and tidy. But definitions built on belief in gods fit some traditions awkwardly. Buddhist teaching, for example, does not center on a creator God, yet scholars widely count Buddhism as a religion.

cards.headline: Definition two: what religion does
cards.body: In 1912 the sociologist Emile Durkheim took the other road. For him a religion is a unified system of beliefs and practices about sacred things, things "set apart and forbidden", which unite everyone who shares them into one moral community. The weight falls on the second half. Scholars call this a functional definition: religion is known by the role it plays, like binding people together. It needs no gods at all, which is exactly why some find it too roomy.

cards.headline: Even the word is local
cards.body: The trouble runs deeper than wording. The concept of religion reached East Asia with scholars only about a century ago, and everyday translations, like Chinese zongjiao, often suggest organized, hierarchical religions rather than traditional practice. In late imperial China a devoted Confucian scholar could join Daoist or Buddhist rituals with no sense of switching sides. Try sorting that into one box. The box, not the people, is what doesn't fit.

learned: Tylor defined religion as belief in spiritual beings
Durkheim defined it by a community united around sacred things
Every definition fits some traditions awkwardly

title: Seven Dimensions of Religion
objective: After this level you can use Ninian Smart's seven dimensions (ritual, story, doctrine, ethics, community, experience, material) to describe any religion beyond its beliefs.
summary: Ninian Smart described religions through seven dimensions: ritual, experience, story, doctrine, ethics, community and material forms, so a description neglects neither ideas nor practices.

cards.headline: Stop asking what religion is. Ask what a religion has.
cards.body: That was Ninian Smart's move. Hunting for one essence behind every religion, he argued, ends in vagueness. So he split religion into its sides, the way a prism splits one beam into colors.

cards.headline: Seven sides of one faith
cards.body: Smart, who became founding professor of religious studies at Lancaster University in 1967, named seven dimensions. Ritual and practice. Experience and emotion. Narrative, the sacred stories. Doctrine and philosophy. Ethics and law. The social side: the community and its institutions. And the material side. Remember Level 1's four shared things? Smart's list keeps them and adds three more.
cards.callout: Ritual, experience, story, doctrine, ethics, community, material

cards.headline: The sides work together
cards.body: The dimensions aren't separate drawers. At Passover, as Jews share the meal, they retrace the story of the Exodus from Egypt: ritual and story bound together, in Smart's words. Feeling runs through everything too. "Ritual without feeling is cold," Smart wrote, and "doctrines without awe or compassion are dry."

cards.headline: Don't forget the stuff
cards.body: The material dimension is the easiest to overlook. It covers buildings, art and the natural places held sacred, like the river Ganges, the Jordan and Mount Fuji. Smart's point was balance: a good description neglects neither ideas nor practices. Judge a religion by its beliefs alone and you've read the menu but skipped the meal.

cards.headline: A test drive on a flag
cards.body: Smart tried his list on nationalism and found many of the dimensions: anthems, flags and memorials. Yet he held that secular worldviews shouldn't really be called religions. The seven dimensions describe; they don't decide what gets the label.

title: Studying Religion Fairly
objective: After this level you can explain how scholars describe what believers hold without judging whether it is true, and why no faith speaks with a single voice.
summary: Scholars bracket the question of truth to describe religions in their own terms; 'myth' in their usage means a sacred story, not a false one; and every tradition is a family of subtraditions.

cards.headline: Can you explain a faith accurately without deciding if it's true?
cards.body: Scholars of religion try to do exactly that. Here's the method, a word that trips people up, and the reason no religion ever speaks with just one voice.

cards.headline: Put truth in brackets
cards.body: Scholars in the phenomenology of religion use a technique called epoché: "bracketing", or suspending judgment. They set aside their own beliefs to describe a religion in its own terms, with empathy for the people who practice it. The question "is it true?" isn't thrown away. It's set aside so the description comes out fair. A believer and a skeptic should both be able to read it and nod.

cards.headline: A myth isn't a mistake
cards.body: Scholars often call a religion's sacred stories myths, and that word trips people up. In everyday speech a myth is something false. In the study of religion, Smart explained, calling a story a myth carries no implication that it is false. And to believers, he added, these narratives are very often history. So when a scholar says "myth", read "sacred story", nothing more.

mascot.line: When you hear "all Christians" or "all Hindus believe", slow down. "Many" or "most" is usually closer to the truth.

cards.headline: No faith speaks with one voice
cards.body: Smart asked readers to picture a Baptist chapel in Georgia, plain, with hymns, Bible reading and fervent preaching, and an Eastern Orthodox church in Romania, glowing with candles and icons, full of processions and chanting. Both are Christian, and both feel like home to their members. Every tradition, Smart wrote, is a loosely held-together family of subtraditions.

cards.headline: Studying Religion Fairly: the takeaways
learned: Scholars bracket the question of truth to describe religions fairly
In the study of religion, a myth is a sacred story, not a false one
Every tradition is a family of subtraditions

title: The Oldest Signs of Belief
objective: After this level you can describe what ancient burials with grave goods and the stone pillars of Göbekli Tepe suggest about religion before writing.
summary: About 100,000 years ago at Qafzeh, people buried their dead with ochre and antlers. Göbekli Tepe's carved pillars, raised by hunter-gatherers, show ritual on a grand scale long before writing.

cards.headline: Writing began around 3200 BCE. Signs of belief are far older.
cards.body: For the long ages before writing, archaeologists read what people left behind. The oldest clues are graves, some about 100,000 years old. The grandest is a hilltop of carved stone pillars.

cards.headline: A child buried with antlers
cards.body: At Qafzeh cave in Israel, about 100,000 years ago, early modern humans buried their dead. Red ochre lay near the bones, which suggests it was used in a ritual. In one grave, a youngster of about 12 or 13 lay in a pit with two deer antlers placed on the chest. Researchers call it a deliberate, ceremonial burial. Someone chose those antlers.

cards.headline: What a grave can and can't tell you
cards.body: Early humans often buried their dead with beads and other symbolic objects. The Smithsonian's scientists suggest these rituals may imply a belief that a person's identity continues beyond death. Notice the "may". A grave keeps the gifts, not the thoughts behind them, so archaeologists speak carefully.

cards.headline: Stone circles before farms
cards.body: In southeastern Turkey, in the 10th to 9th millennium BCE, people who had not yet taken up farming raised Göbekli Tepe. Its T-shaped limestone pillars reach over 5 meters tall and weigh up to 50 tons, and some are carved with foxes, scorpions and lions. Hunter-gatherers built this. Whatever they believed, they believed it enough to move mountains, or at least 50-ton pieces of them.

cards.headline: Temple, town, or both?
cards.body: Its excavator, Klaus Schmidt, saw Göbekli Tepe as a ritual center where no one lived. Newer digs found hearths, houses and a rainwater cistern, so scholars now see a settlement with a religious center. Before writing, the evidence can be read in more than one way, and each season of digging can change the reading.

title: Scripture and Oral Tradition
objective: After this level you can explain what makes a text sacred to a community and how some traditions passed scripture down by memory for centuries.
summary: A scripture is a text a community reveres as carrying sacred power or revelation, gathered into a canon. Most began as oral tradition, like the Vedas and the Buddhist Pali canon.

cards.headline: Some of the world's oldest scriptures spent centuries with no pages at all.
cards.body: Most sacred texts started out spoken, carried in memory from teacher to student. What makes a text sacred, and how do you keep one word-perfect without writing it down?

cards.headline: What makes a text sacred
cards.body: Scriptures are texts a community reveres because they are believed to carry spiritual power, or to be the way a divine being or sacred reality is revealed. Over time the most sacred ones are gathered into a canon: a fixed collection held fully authoritative, settled by general agreement or by official religious bodies. So a text doesn't become scripture by being old or beautiful. It becomes scripture because a community receives it that way.

cards.headline: Memory before ink
cards.body: Most scriptures began as oral traditions, memorized and passed down, generation after generation, until someone wrote them down. The Vedas, which Hindus regard as shruti, "what is heard", were composed from about 1500 BCE, most scholars estimate, and preserved by voice. Reciters are taught from childhood techniques based on tonal accents and exact pronunciation, so the sound of every word stays unaltered. Think of it as a backup system made of people.

cards.headline: Written down, still spoken
cards.body: Buddhist teachings were memorized and recited by monks for generations; the Pali canon was first written down in Sri Lanka, probably in the 1st century BCE. Writing didn't end the spoken life of scripture, though. The Quran's name means "recitation", and verses from it are recited in the five daily prayers.

title: Rites of Passage
objective: After this level you can explain the three stages scholars see in rites of passage, from coming-of-age ceremonies to funerals.
summary: Rites of passage move a person from one status to another. Van Gennep saw three stages: separation, transition and incorporation, visible in a bat mitzvah and a Hindu funeral alike.

cards.headline: Graduations, weddings, funerals: why do big changes come with ceremonies?
cards.body: Every known society marks the big turning points of life. In 1909 a French anthropologist noticed that these ceremonies share a hidden three-part shape.

cards.headline: Ceremonies for crossing over
cards.body: Arnold van Gennep called them rites of passage: ceremonies that move a person from one social or religious status to another. They appear in all known societies, around birth, coming of age, marriage and death. They also do quiet work. They teach people their new roles, reinforce shared values and bring the community together.

cards.headline: Three stages
cards.body: Van Gennep found the same sequence again and again. First, separation: you leave your old status behind. Then transition, the liminal stage, from the Latin limen, "threshold". Finally, incorporation: the community takes you back with your new status. The middle is the strange part. Picture standing in a doorway: out of one room, not yet in the next.

cards.headline: Coming of age
cards.body: Bar and bat mitzvah mean "son" and "daughter of the commandment". Jewish boys usually mark it at 13 and girls at 12 or 13, often with a first public reading from the Torah. In the 20th century the bat mitzvah for girls spread widely, across Conservative, Reform and some Orthodox congregations.

cards.headline: The last rite
cards.body: Hindu funeral rites, antyeshti, vary by caste and sect, but generally involve cremation and placing the ashes in a sacred river. For 10 days the immediate family observe special restrictions and perform rites that many Hindus believe help the soul of the dead on to its next life. A rite of passage, it turns out, carries the living too.

title: Families of Faith
objective: After this level you can sort the world's religions into the Abrahamic, Indian, East Asian and Indigenous families and say what links each family.
summary: The Abrahamic faiths share Abraham; the Indian family shares karma and rebirth; East Asian traditions blend and honor ancestors; Indigenous traditions are many, each tied to its people and place.

cards.headline: Religions have family trees, too.
cards.body: Sorting them into families shows who shares an ancestor, an idea or a homeland. Here are four families, and a warning about the last one.

cards.headline: The Abrahamic family
cards.body: Judaism, Christianity and Islam share reverence for Abraham, who is often considered the first monotheist. They trace the family line differently: Jews and Christians through his son Isaac, Muslims through his son Ishmael. Three faiths, one ancestor.

cards.headline: The Indian family
cards.body: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism all began in the Indian subcontinent, Sikhism in the Punjab in the late 15th century. Running through much of this family is karma, the law by which good or bad actions shape future existence, together with rebirth (samsara) and the hope of release from it (moksha).

cards.headline: The East Asian family
cards.body: In China, religion draws on Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism, often blended with folk traditions; in Japan, Shinto is the indigenous religion. Remember Level 2's Confucian scholar at a Daoist ritual? East Asians, Britannica notes, may call themselves Shintoists, Daoists, Buddhists or Christians, yet seldom stop being Confucians. Honoring ancestors is widespread: in a 2023 survey, roughly half or more of adults everywhere surveyed had made them offerings in the past year.
cards.callout: Linked by: blending traditions, honoring ancestors

cards.headline: Indigenous traditions: many, not one
cards.body: Here's the warning. There is no single "Native American religion". Practices differ from people to people, are often tied to particular places, and are passed on orally. The Menominee, for instance, explain their origins through the geography of their own homeland. "Indigenous" names many traditions, each belonging to its own people and land.

The Indian family shares karma, rebirth and release

title: Counting the World's Believers
objective: After this level you can explain how researchers count religious groups, and roughly how large the biggest groups and the religiously unaffiliated are.
summary: Researchers count religion by what people say in censuses and surveys. In 2020 about 29% of the world was Christian, 26% Muslim and 24% unaffiliated, and 'unaffiliated' doesn't mean unbelieving.

cards.headline: How do you count the believers on an entire planet?
cards.body: No one can look inside every heart. So researchers ask a much simpler question, and add up the answers.

cards.headline: Ask, then add
cards.body: The Pew Research Center's estimates for 2020 draw on more than 2,700 censuses and surveys. Many of them ask a question like "What is your religion, if any?" and researchers sort the answers into broad groups; Christians of every denomination, for example, count as one. So the numbers measure the identity people report, not how often they pray or what they believe.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the decimals. Remember the order: Christians, Muslims, the unaffiliated, Hindus, Buddhists.

cards.headline: The world in 2020
cards.body: About 29% of the world's people were Christian and 26% Muslim. Next came the religiously unaffiliated, about 24%, then Hindus at 15% and Buddhists at 4%. Jews numbered about 15 million. Baha'is, Daoists, Jains, Shintoists, Sikhs and many others together made up about 2%.

cards.headline: "None" isn't the same as no belief
cards.body: The unaffiliated are people who call themselves atheist, agnostic or "nothing in particular". Some of them still hold religious or spiritual beliefs and practices. Remember Level 8's ancestor offerings? In Pew's 2023 survey, 92% of religiously unaffiliated adults in Vietnam had made an offering to ancestors in the past year. The survey box says none; the offering says otherwise.

cards.headline: Where counting gets hard
cards.body: Some countries don't ask at all. Since a 1976 law, the US census may not require anyone to answer questions about religious beliefs or membership, so American religion figures come from private surveys instead.

title: Abraham and the Covenant
objective: After this level you can explain the covenant Jews believe God made with Abraham, and why Judaism, Christianity and Islam all honor him.
summary: Jews believe God made an everlasting covenant with Abraham, promising land and descendants, with circumcision as its sign. Judaism, Christianity and Islam all trace their story to him.

cards.headline: Three of the world's faiths trace their story to one man on the move.
cards.body: Judaism, Christianity and Islam all honor Abraham. For Jews he is where something specific begins: a covenant, a binding bond with God. Here is what Genesis says was promised, and the sign that still marks it.

cards.headline: Pack up, destination unknown
cards.body: Genesis tells how God spoke to Abram: "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto the land that I will show thee." He left Ur, in Mesopotamia, and only later learned the land was Canaan. Picture loading the car with no address in the map app. Abraham is best known for exactly this: the depth of his faith.

cards.headline: A covenant, not a contract
cards.body: A covenant (Hebrew berit) is a binding agreement, and in this one God binds himself by oath. Jewish tradition holds that God promised Abraham the land of Canaan and descendants beyond counting. Genesis even renames him: Abram becomes Abraham, "the father of a multitude of nations." And it calls the bond "an everlasting covenant", for Abraham "and thy seed after thee throughout their generations."

cards.headline: A sign in the body
cards.body: Genesis 17 names the covenant's sign: every male is to be circumcised, "a token of a covenant", at eight days old. Jewish families still hold the rite, berit mila (often spelled brit milah), on a baby boy's eighth day, with blessings and the giving of his name. In Judaism it represents the fulfillment of the covenant between God and Abraham. One promise, marked again in each generation.

cards.headline: Three faiths, one ancestor

In Islam, the Prophet Muhammad is a descendant of Ishmael; in Christianity, the genealogy of Jesus is traced to Isaac. One ancestor, three family stories, each told in its own words.

title: Moses, Exodus and Sinai
objective: After this level you can retell the Exodus as Jews tell it, explain the giving of the Torah at Sinai, and say what historians can and cannot confirm.
summary: Moses led the Israelites out of Egyptian slavery to Sinai, where Jews believe God gave the Torah. Archaeology has not confirmed the story; Israel is first named about 1205 BCE.

cards.headline: It is the story Jews retell at every Passover meal.
cards.body: Slaves walk out of Egypt, and at a mountain in the desert they receive a law. Here is the story as the Bible tells it, what it means to Jews, and what historians can and can't say about it.

cards.headline: Out of Egypt
cards.body: In the biblical account, a pharaoh enslaved the Hebrews in Egypt. After a series of plagues struck the land, he let them go, and Moses led them through the Red Sea, which, the Bible says, God parted for them. No wonder Jewish tradition reveres Moses as its greatest prophet and teacher.

cards.headline: A law that begins with a rescue
cards.body: At Mount Sinai, the Bible tells, God made the Israelites his people and gave them the terms of his covenant, including the Ten Commandments. Notice how they open: "I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." The law starts by recalling a rescue. Many Jews also hold that an Oral Torah, laws and customs passed down by word of mouth, was revealed to Moses.

cards.headline: What historians can say
cards.body: Archaeology has not confirmed the Exodus as the Bible describes it. The Bible scholar S. David Sperling notes there is no archaeological evidence that the Israelites were ever in Egypt. The earliest widely accepted mention of Israel is an inscription of the pharaoh Merneptah from about 1205 BCE. Some historians still think an escape by part of Israel's ancestors lies behind the story, given how central it became to Israel's faith.

title: The Hebrew Bible
objective: After this level you can name the three parts of the Tanakh and explain how the Torah is read aloud in the synagogue through the year.
summary: The Tanakh has three parts, Torah, Neviim and Ketuvim, in 24 books. The Torah, its first five books, is handwritten on a scroll and read aloud through the year, ending and restarting on Simchat Torah.

cards.headline: Every synagogue keeps its holiest book as a handwritten scroll.
cards.body: Not printed, not on a screen: written by hand on parchment. What's inside it, how does it fit into the whole Hebrew Bible, and why does the reading never really end?

cards.headline: Three parts, one name
cards.body: Jews call their Bible the Tanakh, an acronym of its three parts: Torah (Instruction, or Law), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings). The Hebrew canon counts 24 books, one for each scroll they were written on in ancient times. Christians later split some, like Samuel and Kings, into two each, and the Minor Prophets into 12, so the same writings add up to more books in Christian Bibles.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. The Torah is the first five books; the Tanakh is the whole Hebrew Bible. The Torah sits inside the Tanakh.

cards.headline: The scroll in the ark
cards.body: The Torah is the first part: the five books of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. In the synagogue it lives in the ark as a Sefer Torah, written in Hebrew by a qualified scribe, a sofer, on parchment. It is read aloud on Sabbaths, Mondays, Thursdays and festivals, and carried out and back with deep reverence.

cards.headline: The reading that never ends
cards.body: A congregation reads through the Torah in a yearly cycle. On the festival of Simchat Torah, the last part of Deuteronomy is read, and then, right away, the first part of Genesis. People carry the scrolls in seven circles around the reading platform, dancing. The last page and the first page, on the same morning.

title: Temple, Exile and Return
objective: After this level you can explain how the destruction of the Jerusalem Temple in 586 BCE and again in 70 CE reshaped Jewish life.
summary: Babylon destroyed the First Temple in 586 BCE; exiles kept faith through the Sabbath and prayer. The rebuilt Temple fell to Rome in 70 CE; the Western Wall and Tisha b'Av keep its memory.

cards.headline: Twice, the center of Jewish worship was destroyed.
cards.body: The Temple in Jerusalem became the only place of sacrifice in Judah. It was lost in 586 BCE, rebuilt, and lost again in 70 CE. Each loss changed how Jews lived their faith.

cards.headline: The First Temple falls
cards.body: The First Temple was completed under King Solomon in the 10th century BCE, and in time it became the only place of sacrifice in Judah. Then, in 586 BCE, the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple, and many Judeans were deported to Babylonia. Imagine your whole religious life built around one building, and then the building is gone.

cards.headline: Faith by the rivers of Babylon
cards.body: In exile, Jews kept the Sabbath and holy days, practiced circumcision and offered prayers in place of the Temple's sacrifices. Some scholars think synagogues began then. A psalm keeps the grief: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion." Without knowing it, the exiles were practicing Judaism without a Temple.

cards.headline: Return, and a second loss
cards.body: In 538 BCE Cyrus the Great, the Persian king who had conquered Babylonia, let the Jews go home, though some chose to stay. The rebuilt Temple was completed in 515 BCE. It stood for centuries, until the Romans destroyed it in 70 CE, during a Jewish rebellion against Rome.

cards.headline: What remains
cards.body: The Western Wall is a surviving stretch of the wall that ringed the Temple Mount. It is a place of prayer, where people push slips of paper with prayers into the cracks. Each July or August, on the fast of Tisha b'Av, many Jews mourn both Temples and read the Book of Lamentations.

title: From Temple to Rabbis
objective: After this level you can explain how rabbis, synagogues and the Talmud let Judaism thrive without a Temple, in a worldwide diaspora.
summary: After 70 CE, the Yavneh academy and the synagogue carried Judaism on through prayer, study and a minyan of ten. The oral law, gathered in the Mishnah, grew into the Talmud.

cards.headline: The Temple was gone. How do you keep a religion going without its center?
cards.body: In 70 CE the Romans destroyed the Second Temple, the only place for Jewish sacrifices. The answer that followed needed no building in Jerusalem at all: teachers, prayer and a library of arguments.

cards.headline: Out in a coffin
cards.body: Rabbi Johanan ben Zakkai's disciples are credited with smuggling their teacher out of Jerusalem in a coffin. He set up an academy at Jabneh (Yavneh), and ruled that ceremonies once limited to the Temple could be kept elsewhere, "to serve as memorials of the Sanctuary." With that, he fixed the conditions for Judaism to carry on after the Temple.

cards.headline: Ten people, anywhere
cards.body: The synagogue became the focal point of Jewish religious life. Its Hebrew names say what it's for: house of prayer, house of assembly, house of study. Its worship has no sacrifice, so it needs no priest. It needs a minyan, a quorum of ten, traditionally men (Reform and Conservative Judaism also count women); without one, there is no public Torah reading. That suited the Diaspora, Jewish communities scattered far beyond the land.

mascot.line: Keep this pair straight: the Mishnah is the core text; the Talmud is the Mishnah plus the Gemara's debates about it.

cards.headline: A library of arguments
cards.body: By 100 CE, rabbi, "my teacher", meant a sage who interprets Jewish law. Early in the 3rd century, Judah ha-Nasi gave final form to the Mishnah, the oldest authoritative collection of Jewish oral law. Later sages added the Gemara, a commentary, and together they make up the Talmud, where scholars debate every text to wring out its meaning.

title: Shabbat
objective: After this level you can explain how and why many Jews keep a weekly day of rest from Friday evening to Saturday night.
summary: Shabbat runs from sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday, recalling God resting on the seventh day. It opens with candles, wine and two challah loaves and closes with havdalah.

cards.headline: One day a week, many Jews stop working on purpose.
cards.body: For about a day, the week's work is set aside. Where does that come from, what exactly stops, and what fills the time instead?

cards.headline: A palace in time
cards.body: Shabbat runs from sunset on Friday to nightfall on Saturday. Genesis says God "rested on the seventh day from all His work", and it is the only Jewish holiday in the Ten Commandments: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." In his 1951 book The Sabbath, Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel called it "a palace in time": holiness you enter by the calendar, not through a door.

cards.headline: What stops
cards.body: The Talmud lists 39 general categories of forbidden work, including cooking and baking. But the rules give way when life or health is seriously at risk. Practice varies: Orthodox Jews strive to keep the day in full, while Conservative and Reform Jews vary in how they observe it.

cards.headline: Candles, wine and two loaves
cards.body: Before sunset on Friday, traditionally the woman of the house lights the Sabbath candles. Dinner opens with Kiddush, a blessing of sanctification over wine, and two loaves of challah, recalling the double portion of manna the Bible says God gave in the wilderness. On Saturday night, havdalah, with blessings over wine, spices and a braided candle, separates the holy day from the ordinary week.

title: The Jewish Year
objective: After this level you can explain the meaning and customs of Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Passover, Sukkot and Hanukkah.
summary: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur bring the shofar, repentance and a fast. Sukkot recalls the wilderness, Passover retells the Exodus, Hanukkah remembers a rededicated Temple.

cards.headline: The Jewish year opens with a blast on a ram's horn.
cards.body: Then come ten serious days, meals in a hut, a dinner full of questions and eight nights of lights. Each festival tells part of the Jewish story.

cards.headline: New year, clean slate
cards.body: Rosh Hashanah, the religious New Year, falls on 1 Tishri, in September or October. The shofar, a ram's horn, sounds a call to spiritual reawakening. It opens the Ten Days of Repentance, which end on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement: the holiest day of the year, with a 25-hour fast and prayer. Beforehand, friends ask each other's forgiveness, since forgiveness from people signifies forgiveness from God.

cards.headline: A hut and a question-filled dinner
cards.body: Five days after Yom Kippur comes Sukkot. Families eat, and some even sleep, in huts roofed with branches, recalling the Israelites' 40 years in the wilderness. In March or April, Passover remembers the escape from slavery in Egypt: at the seder, people read the story from the Haggadah, and children ask, "Why does this night differ from all other nights?" Matzah recalls dough that had no time to rise.

cards.headline: Eight nights of light
cards.body: Hanukkah, "dedication", remembers the Maccabees rededicating the Second Temple in 164 BCE. One more candle is lit each night for eight nights, and the Talmud tells of oil that burned for eight days. Big glow, small holiday: it has traditionally counted as minor, and it isn't in the Hebrew Bible.

title: Kosher and the Commandments
objective: After this level you can explain the mitzvot, the commandments Jews follow, using the basic rules of keeping kosher as the example.
summary: The Talmud counts 613 commandments (mitzvot) in the Torah. Keeping kosher shows how they work: permitted animals, ritual slaughter, and meat kept apart from milk.

cards.headline: Why would a cheeseburger break a religious law?
cards.body: For Jews who keep kosher, the problem isn't the beef or the cheese. It's the two together. That rule is one of 613 commandments, and it shows how they shape an ordinary dinner.

cards.headline: 613 commandments
cards.body: A mitzvah is a commandment in the Torah, to be kept by every practicing Jew. The Talmud counts 613: 248 to do and 365 not to do, as many don'ts as there are days in a year. Rabbis added more over the centuries, such as lighting candles on certain festivals. And Jews count any good deed as fulfilling a mitzvah, because it expresses God's will.

cards.headline: Which animals
cards.body: Kosher means "fit" or "proper". Jews who keep kosher eat only mammals that chew the cud and have cloven feet, fish with both fins and scales, and certain birds. The Torah permits "the ox, the sheep, and the goat" but not the swine, which "parteth the hoof" yet "cheweth not the cud." Meat must come from a ritual slaughter, and blood is drawn out by soaking and salting.

cards.headline: Meat and milk apart
cards.body: Three times the Torah says, "Thou shalt not seethe a kid in its mother's milk." From it comes the strict separation of meat and dairy, in eating and in cooking, with separate sets of dishes and utensils. Why these rules? For observant Jews, no reason is needed beyond this: God commanded them.

cards.headline: Same rules, many kitchens
cards.body: In Pew's 2020 survey of US Jews, 17% said they keep kosher at home: 95% of Orthodox Jews, 24% of Conservative Jews and 5% of Reform Jews. Same commandments, very different kitchens.

title: Branches of Judaism Today
objective: After this level you can compare Orthodox, Conservative and Reform Judaism, and tell these branches apart from Ashkenazi and Sephardi heritage.
summary: Orthodox, Conservative and Reform Judaism differ over how binding traditional Jewish law is. Ashkenazi and Sephardi describe family heritage and custom, not branches of belief.

cards.headline: Orthodox or Reform? Ashkenazi or Sephardi? Two different questions.
cards.body: One is about how binding Jewish law is today. The other is about where a family's customs come from. Let's take them one at a time.

cards.headline: Orthodox: the law stands
cards.body: Orthodox Judaism holds that the Written Law, the Torah, and the Oral Law, set down in the Mishnah and interpreted in the Talmud, are fixed and remain the sole guide for religious life. Orthodox Jews keep daily worship, kashrut, traditional prayers and intensive Torah study, with men and women seated apart in the synagogue.

cards.headline: Reform and Conservative
cards.body: Reform Judaism began early in the 19th century in Germany; its first services, in 1810, brought an organ, a choir and prayers in German. It teaches that Judaism is a living, developing faith, and questions the binding force of ritual law. Conservative Judaism, inspired by Zacharias Frankel, treats the Law as sacred and living, and changes it more slowly; since 1985 it has ordained women as rabbis.

cards.headline: Who belongs where
cards.body: In Pew's 2020 survey of US Jews, 37% identified as Reform, 17% as Conservative and 9% as Orthodox, with about 4% in other branches. And 32% named no branch at all.

mascot.line: Branch answers "how do you practice?" Heritage answers "where is your family from?" Keep the two apart.

cards.headline: Heritage is a different question
cards.body: Ashkenazim descend from Jews of the Rhineland and France who moved east to lands like Poland and Lithuania; many spoke Yiddish. Sephardim descend from the Jews of Spain and Portugal, and many kept Judeo-Spanish, Ladino. Jews of North Africa and the Middle East are more properly called Mizrahim. Their customs differ, but as a matter of tradition, not of sect.

title: Jesus of Nazareth
objective: After this level you can separate what historians generally accept about Jesus, a Jewish teacher from Galilee, from what Christians believe about him.
summary: Historians accept that Jesus was a Jewish teacher from Galilee, baptized by John and crucified under Pontius Pilate around 30 CE; Christians believe he is the Christ who rose from the dead.

cards.headline: Jesus was not a Christian.
cards.body: He was a Jew from Galilee, and the faith named after him took shape later. So there are two ways to talk about him: what historians can show, and what Christians believe. This level keeps them side by side.

cards.headline: What historians accept
cards.body: Most historians accept a short list. Jesus was a Jew from Nazareth in Galilee, born about 6 to 4 BCE, a traveling teacher, prophet and healer. As a young adult he was baptized by the prophet John the Baptist. His central message was the kingdom of God, often taught in parables. Around 30 CE, in Jerusalem, he was crucified on the orders of Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judaea from 26 to 36 CE.

cards.headline: How they know
cards.body: The main sources are the four Gospels of the New Testament. Historians also have a witness from outside: the Roman historian Tacitus, no admirer of Christians. In his Annals he wrote that Christus, the founder of the Christians' name, was put to death under the emperor Tiberius by sentence of Pontius Pilate, and he called the movement a "pernicious superstition". A hostile source confirming the ending is gold to a historian.

mascot.line: Keep the labels straight: "historians accept" the crucifixion, "Christians believe" the resurrection. Level 4's bracketing at work.

cards.headline: What Christians believe
cards.body: Christ isn't a surname. It's a title, from the Greek christos, which translates the Hebrew meshiah, Messiah: "the anointed one". Jesus's disciples became convinced that he rose from the dead and appeared to them, and Christians believe he did. Most Christians regard him as the Incarnation of God, God made human. Same person, two kinds of statement.

title: The New Testament
objective: After this level you can explain what the Gospels and Paul's letters are and how the New Testament canon took shape over about three centuries.
summary: Paul's letters came first; the Gospels followed after about 40 years of oral retelling, Mark around 70 CE; in 367 Athanasius listed the 27 books of today's New Testament.

cards.headline: For about 40 years after Jesus died, there was no written Gospel.
cards.body: His followers told and retold his story aloud. So how did that become a collection of 27 books, and who decided which ones?

cards.headline: Paul writes first
cards.body: The oldest books of the New Testament aren't the Gospels. They're Paul's letters, written to young churches about their immediate problems, soon after Jesus's death. They sit after the Gospels anyway: the 27 books (four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, the letters and Revelation) aren't in the order they were written. All of them are in Koine, the Greek then used from Greece to the Middle East.

cards.headline: Then the Gospels
cards.body: Gospel comes from the Old English god-spell, translating the Greek euangelion: "good news". Most scholars agree Mark wrote first, around 70 CE, weaving together stories Christians had been retelling aloud since Jesus's death around 30 CE. Matthew and Luke used Mark as a source. None of the writers was out to satisfy historical curiosity, Britannica notes. They wrote to bear witness to a faith.

cards.headline: Drawing the line
cards.body: Other early Christian writings circulated too, and churches argued over which counted. In 367 CE, Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, sent his churches a letter listing exactly today's 27 books, the first time that list appears. He meant to end disputes over texts like the Shepherd of Hermas, which some had treated as equal to the apostles' letters. From Jesus's death to that list: more than three centuries. Christians place these books after the Jewish scriptures, which they call the Old Testament.

title: The Trinity and the Creeds
objective: After this level you can explain the Christian belief in one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and how the Nicene Creed set it out.
summary: Christians believe in one God in three persons; the Nicene Creed calls the Son 'of one substance' with the Father and is shared across the major churches.

cards.headline: One God, three persons: how do Christians hold both at once?
cards.body: They call it the Trinity. Here's what the teaching says, the single Greek word that defined it, and why churches still say it aloud in worship.

cards.headline: Three persons, one God
cards.body: The Trinity is the Christian teaching of the unity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit as three persons in one Godhead. The point is one God, not three. Neither the word "Trinity" nor the doctrine spelled out appears in the New Testament. Christians worked it out from their scriptures over the following centuries, and by the end of the 4th century it had taken substantially the form it has kept ever since.

cards.headline: One word draws the line
cards.body: The sharpest test came from Arius, who taught that Christ was not divine but a created being. In 325 the Council of Nicaea condemned that teaching. Its creed called the Son homoousios with the Father, Greek for "of one substance": fully equal, not a lesser being. The text most churches now call the Nicene Creed was issued at a later council, in Constantinople in 381.

cards.headline: Said aloud, together
cards.body: A creed is an authoritative summary of a community's beliefs, brief enough to say in worship. The Nicene Creed is the only one accepted as authoritative by Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anglican and major Protestant churches: one text, shared. With one difference. From the 6th century, Western churches gradually added "and the Son" to its line on the Holy Spirit, and Eastern churches have always rejected it.

title: Baptism and Communion
objective: After this level you can explain how Christians practice baptism and Communion and why churches understand them differently.
summary: Baptism with water admits a person to the church, as an infant or as a professing believer; Communion recalls the Last Supper, and churches differ on what happens to the bread and wine.

cards.headline: Water, bread and wine: Christianity's two great rituals.
cards.body: Churches practice both, and practice them differently. Who should be baptized? What happens to the bread? The answers show what each church believes.

cards.headline: Baptism: the way in
cards.body: Baptism is Christianity's rite of admission. Water is used, by full immersion, pouring or sprinkling, with the words "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit". Paul described it as sharing in Christ's death, burial and resurrection. Picture the full-immersion version: going under, coming back up.

cards.headline: Babies or believers?
cards.body: Most traditional churches, including Catholic, Lutheran, Anglican and Reformed, baptize infants. Baptists and some others baptize only people old enough to profess their faith themselves, a practice rooted in the Anabaptists of the Reformation. Both agree baptism starts a Christian life. They disagree on whether the person's own faith must come first.

cards.headline: Communion: a remembered meal
cards.body: The Eucharist, from the Greek for "thanksgiving", is also called Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper. It commemorates Jesus's Last Supper, when, the Gospels say, he blessed bread and wine and told his disciples to repeat it in his memory. For most churches it is the central act of worship.

cards.headline: What's in the cup?
cards.body: Here churches part ways. Catholics teach transubstantiation: the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood while still looking like bread and wine. Orthodox Christians affirm Christ's real presence in their own terms. Lutherans affirm a real presence too, but not transubstantiation. The Swiss reformer Zwingli saw a memorial, and some churches call it an ordinance rather than a sacrament.

title: Christmas, Lent and Easter
objective: After this level you can explain the shape of the Christian year and why the date of Easter moves from year to year.
summary: The church year runs through a Christmas cycle and an Easter cycle; Lent's 40 days prepare for Easter, which follows the first full moon on or after March 21, so it moves.

cards.headline: Christmas never moves. Easter can land on any Sunday in a five-week window.
cards.body: Christmas is always December 25; Easter falls anywhere from March 22 to April 25. The reason is the Moon, and it shows how the whole Christian year is built.

cards.headline: A year that tells one story
cards.body: The church year is an annual cycle centered on Christ's life, death and resurrection, and it has two halves. The Christmas cycle opens with Advent, the four Sundays before Christmas, then celebrates his birth on December 25 and continues to Epiphany. The Easter cycle runs through Lent and Holy Week to Easter and Pentecost. Live through one year and you've walked the whole story.

cards.headline: Easter at the center
cards.body: Easter celebrates the resurrection of Jesus, which Christians believe happened on the third day after his crucifixion. It shaped the calendar from the start: early Christians kept every Sunday as "the Lord's day" in its memory, and the 50 days from Easter to Pentecost framed the first church year. Everything else in the year is arranged around it.

cards.headline: Lent: forty days of getting ready
cards.body: Lent is a 40-day season of penitence before Easter, recalling Jesus's fast in the wilderness. Western churches begin it on Ash Wednesday; Orthodox Great Lent begins on Clean Monday. Christians keep it with fasting, abstinence and giving to others, and many also give up a pleasure, like sweets, alcohol or social media. Yes, social media counts.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the range. Remember the recipe: spring equinox, then full moon, then the next Sunday.

cards.headline: Why Easter moves
cards.body: Western churches keep Easter on the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox, fixed for this purpose at March 21. So the earliest possible Easter is March 22 and the latest is April 25. Orthodox churches calculate it by the older Julian calendar, which is why their Easter usually comes later.

title: The Catholic Church
objective: After this level you can explain how the Catholic Church is organized under the pope and bishops, and what its seven sacraments are.
summary: The Catholic Church, the largest Christian church, is led by the pope as bishop of Rome, with bishops over dioceses and parishes; cardinals elect popes, and seven sacraments mark the Christian life.

cards.headline: About 1.3 billion people belong to one church with one leader.
cards.body: That's the Catholic Church, the largest Christian church. How does something that size hold together? Through a structure that runs from your local parish all the way to Rome.

cards.headline: The bishop of Rome
cards.body: The pope is the bishop of Rome. The Catholic Church teaches that St. Peter was the first pope, and regards every pope since as Peter's successor, with full authority over the whole church in matters of faith and morals. So the most famous title in the church is, first of all, a local one: bishop of one city.

cards.headline: Bishops, dioceses, parishes
cards.body: Below the pope, the church is a map of territories. A diocese is an area run by a bishop, divided into parishes, the local churches. Catholics trace an unbroken line from the apostles through their bishops, called apostolic succession. Only the pope can create, divide or merge dioceses.

cards.headline: White smoke
cards.body: When a new pope is needed, cardinals under 80 meet in a conclave in the Sistine Chapel. A candidate needs two-thirds of the votes. After each round the ballots are burned: black smoke means no decision yet, white smoke means there's a new pope.

cards.headline: Seven sacraments
cards.body: Catholics celebrate seven sacraments: baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist, reconciliation (penance), anointing of the sick, marriage and holy orders. St. Augustine called a sacrament "the visible form of an invisible grace". Protestant reformers generally kept only two: baptism and the Lord's Supper.

title: Eastern Orthodoxy
objective: After this level you can explain what sets Orthodox Christianity apart, from its self-governing churches to icons and its own date for Easter.
summary: Orthodoxy is a communion of self-governing churches with the Ecumenical Patriarch as 'first among equals'; icons are venerated, not worshipped; and Easter follows the Julian calendar.

cards.headline: A family of churches with no single head.
cards.body: Orthodox Christians live mainly in the Balkans, the Middle East and the former Soviet countries. How do their churches hold together with no pope? Here's the answer, plus icons and a second Easter.

cards.headline: Self-governing churches
cards.body: Eastern Orthodoxy is a communion of autocephalous, meaning self-governing, churches. Some are ancient patriarchates: Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem. Others are national churches, like those of Russia, Serbia, Romania and Greece. Think of a family of households that share one faith, each running its own home.

cards.headline: First among equals
cards.body: The Patriarch of Constantinople, called the Ecumenical Patriarch, is "first among equals": an honor, not a pope's authority over the other churches. That difference over authority, with the dispute over the added "and the Son" from Level 23, helped separate East and West in the schism of 1054.

cards.headline: Windows, not idols
cards.body: Icons, images of Christ, the Virgin Mary and the saints, hold a central place in Orthodox churches and in Orthodox homes. Orthodox teaching separates the veneration given to an icon, honor that passes to the person shown, from worship, which is due to God alone. Worship centers on the Divine Liturgy, usually held in national languages, though some churches keep older liturgical ones.

cards.headline: A different Easter
cards.body: Orthodox churches still calculate Easter by the Julian calendar, so their Easter usually falls later than the Western one. Same kind of rule, different calendar.

title: The Protestant Reformation
objective: After this level you can explain how Martin Luther's protest in 1517 split Western Christianity and what "scripture alone" and "faith alone" mean.
summary: In 1517 Luther challenged indulgences; print spread his teaching of faith alone and scripture alone, and Western Christianity split into new Protestant churches.

cards.headline: History's most famous church door may never have had anything nailed to it.
cards.body: In the familiar story, Martin Luther hammers his Ninety-five Theses to a church door in 1517. What historians can prove is plainer, and it still split Western Christianity.

mascot.line: Remember the date and the challenge, not the hammer. The theses changed history however they went public.

cards.headline: A letter, then a legend
cards.body: On October 31, 1517, the German theologian Martin Luther challenged the church's practice of indulgences in his Ninety-five Theses, and sent them to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz. That much is certain. The door-posting story was first recorded nearly 30 years later, by his colleague Philipp Melanchthon, and Luther himself never mentioned it. Historians still debate whether the theses were posted at all.

cards.headline: Faith alone, scripture alone
cards.body: Luther's answer to indulgences was sola fide, "faith alone": salvation is a gift God grants to sinners who have faith in Christ, not something earned by good works. His measure for every church teaching was sola scriptura, "scripture alone". He translated the Bible into German, so lay people depended less on church authority to know what it said.

cards.headline: Printed fast, split for good
cards.body: Printers reprinted Luther's ideas within weeks, and copies were read across Europe. Pope Leo X excommunicated him on January 3, 1521; that April, at the Diet of Worms, he refused to recant unless shown wrong by Scripture or reason. Western Christianity split. Lutheran, Reformed (Calvinist), Anglican and Anabaptist churches grew out of the Reformation; Henry VIII founded the Church of England in 1534.

title: Christianity Goes Global
objective: After this level you can explain how Christianity's center of gravity shifted to Africa, Latin America and Asia, and why Pentecostal churches grew so fast.
summary: In 1910 two-thirds of Christians lived in Europe; by 2020 sub-Saharan Africa held the most. Pentecostal churches grew through lay leadership and evangelism.

cards.headline: Where does the largest share of Christians live? No longer in Europe.
cards.body: By 2020 the answer was sub-Saharan Africa. This level follows the shift, and the fast-growing churches that rode it.

cards.headline: A century-long shift
cards.body: In 1910, about two-thirds of the world's Christians lived in Europe. By 2010, only about a quarter did. By 2020, Pew found, sub-Saharan Africa had overtaken Europe as home to the most Christians: about 31% of the world's Christians, against 24% in Latin America and the Caribbean and 22% in Europe.

cards.headline: How the center moved
cards.body: Two forces did it, Pew explains. Fertility rates are much higher in Africa than in Europe, so African Christian communities grew fast. And in Western Europe, many people stopped identifying as Christian. Growth at one end, departures at the other.

cards.headline: Churches of the Spirit
cards.body: Pentecostalism takes its name from Pentecost, when, as the Acts of the Apostles describes, the Holy Spirit descended on the first Christians in Jerusalem. Pentecostals seek a later experience called baptism with the Holy Spirit, usually with speaking in tongues, and value gifts like prophecy and healing. With charismatics in other churches, they made up about 27% of the world's Christians in 2010.

cards.headline: Why they spread
cards.body: Pentecostals believe God, through the Holy Spirit, acts directly in everyday life, not just in church history. They have long treated spreading the faith as every Christian's job, not a few professionals', and they encouraged lay leadership early. That's a movement built to multiply.

title: Muhammad and the Revelation
objective: After this level you can explain what Muslims believe about Muhammad and the revelation that began in 610, and why the hijra of 622 starts the Islamic calendar.
summary: Muslims believe that in 610 the angel Gabriel ordered Muhammad to recite; Khadijah was the first to believe, and the hijra of 622 became Year 1 of the Islamic calendar.

cards.headline: A cave, a voice and one command: "Recite!"
cards.body: In 610, Muhammad of Mecca was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira. Muslims believe what happened there began the Quran. A journey twelve years later became Year 1 of the Islamic calendar.

cards.headline: The night of "Recite!"
cards.body: Muhammad was born about 570 in Mecca. Muslims believe that in 610, as he meditated in a cave on Mount Hira, the angel Gabriel came to him and ordered him to recite. Words came that Muhammad believed were God's own. The revelations kept coming for the rest of his life, and, remembered and written down, they became the Quran.

cards.headline: The first to believe
cards.body: Khadijah, a merchant who had hired Muhammad to lead a caravan to Syria and later married him, is often considered the first person to believe his message. She reassured him that his first revelations were real. Then he began to preach: there is no god but God, and life should be lived in submission to God's will. That is the word itself. Islam means "surrender", and a Muslim is one who surrenders to God's will.

mascot.line: Two dates, easy to swap. 610 is the first revelation; 622 is the hijra, and Year 1 of the Islamic calendar.

cards.headline: 622: Year One
cards.body: The message drew crowds, and Mecca's powerful saw Muhammad's popularity as a threat. In 622 he and his followers migrated north to Yathrib, later called Medina. Muslims call this move the hijra, "migration", and it mattered so much that the Islamic calendar counts its years from it. Muhammad led the young community until his death in 632.

cards.headline: A messenger, not a god
cards.body: Remember Level 8's Abrahamic family? Muslims see Muhammad as the last in a line of prophets that includes Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Solomon and Jesus. The Quran presents him as a human being with no divine qualities. In Islamic tradition he is God's messenger and the "seal of the prophets": the last of the line, not an object of worship.

title: The Quran
objective: After this level you can explain how the Quran is organized into suras and why Muslims treat its recitation in Arabic as central.
summary: The Quran's 114 suras run roughly from longest to shortest; Muslims believe it is God's speech in Arabic, so they learn to recite it in Arabic and keep it by heart and by voice.

cards.headline: The Quran's name is a verb in disguise.
cards.body: It means "recitation", and its verses are recited in the five daily prayers. So how is the book put together, and why does its sound matter so much?

cards.headline: 114 suras, longest first
cards.body: The Quran is divided into 114 chapter-like units called suras, and each sura into verses called ayat, a word that means "sign". The order surprises newcomers: it isn't the order in which Muslims believe the suras were revealed. After a short opening sura, recited in every one of the five daily prayers, the suras run roughly from longest to shortest. Start at the front and the long ones come first.

cards.headline: God's words, in Arabic
cards.body: Muslims traditionally believe the Quran is a literal transcript of God's speech, revealed to Muhammad in stages, in Arabic, over 23 years. That belief shapes how it is read. Muslims are taught to learn and recite it in Arabic even when Arabic isn't their language. A translation can help a reader understand, but it isn't treated as the Quran itself.

cards.headline: Kept by heart and by voice
cards.body: Muslims believe the standard written text was set shortly after Muhammad's death, under the caliph Uthman. Memory guarded it too: someone who learns the whole Quran by heart is called a hafiz. And recitation is an art. At popular competitions, renowned reciters, women and men, show skills mastered over years. You can read the Quran silently, but it was made to be heard.

title: One God and Six Beliefs
objective: After this level you can explain tawhid, the oneness of God, and the six articles of faith that Muslims hold.
summary: Tawhid, the oneness of God, is the root of Muslim belief; from it grow six articles of faith: God, angels, holy books, prophets, the Day of Judgement and God's decree.

cards.headline: Islam's creed begins with a no.
cards.body: "There is no god but God, and Muhammad is his messenger." Before it tells you what to believe, it clears the field. That testimony expresses tawhid, and everything in this level grows from it.

cards.headline: Tawhid: God is one
cards.body: Tawhid means "making one" or "asserting oneness". Muslims believe God is a unity, not made of parts, with no children, no parents and no partners, and no shape or form that can be seen. Its opposite is shirk, associating anything else with God. In Muslim teaching it is the one sin God will not forgive in the hereafter.

cards.headline: Allah: the Arabic word for God
cards.body: Allah is the standard Arabic word for God, probably a contraction of al-Ilah, "the God". It isn't a word only Muslims use: Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews say Allah too. So when you hear a Muslim say Allah, you can simply hear "God".

cards.headline: Six articles of faith
cards.body: From tawhid grow six main beliefs that Muslims hold. God is one. Angels exist, even if people cannot see them. God revealed holy books. God sent prophets, from Adam and Abraham to Moses and Jesus, with Muhammad the last. A Day of Judgement will come. And God knows all that will happen, which Muslims believe does not stop people from choosing freely.
cards.callout: God, angels, books, prophets, Judgement Day, God's decree

cards.headline: Shared beliefs, many voices
cards.body: How widely are these beliefs held? In Pew surveys of Muslims in 39 countries, belief in one God and in Muhammad as his Prophet was nearly unanimous in most. Belief in fate varied far more: under half in Albania, over nine in ten in Azerbaijan and Turkey. That's Level 4 again: no faith speaks with a single voice.

title: The Five Pillars
objective: After this level you can name the Five Pillars of Islam and explain how together they shape a Muslim's day, year and life.
summary: The shahada, salat, zakat, sawm and hajj run on three clocks: prayer every day, zakat and the Ramadan fast every year, the hajj once in a lifetime.

cards.headline: Five duties, three clocks: the day, the year and a lifetime.
cards.body: Islam gives its central practices a builder's name: pillars. Each runs on its own clock, and together they turn belief into a way of living.

cards.headline: The five
cards.body: The Five Pillars of Islam are the shahada, the profession of faith; salat, prayer five times a day; zakat, giving to the poor; sawm, fasting in the month of Ramadan; and hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca. Islam regards faith without practice as pointless, so the pillars give a Muslim's life its framework, weaving everyday activities and beliefs into one cloth of devotion.

cards.headline: The first pillar opens the door
cards.body: The shahada is Level 33's testimony: "There is no god but God, and Muhammad is his messenger." Reciting it sincerely is all a person needs to do to become a Muslim. One sentence, and the other four pillars follow.

cards.headline: A day, a year, a lifetime
cards.body: Salat comes round five times every day. Zakat comes once a year: 2.5 percent of one's wealth, such as savings above a minimum threshold, given to benefit the poor. Sawm fills one month of every year, Ramadan. And the hajj is due at least once in a lifetime, for every adult Muslim who is physically and financially able.
cards.callout: Daily: salat. Yearly: zakat, sawm. Once: hajj

cards.headline: Giving as worship
cards.body: Zakat isn't a tip left out of kindness. Muslims regard it as a form of worship and of self-purification, and as a reminder that wealth is held on loan from God. Handing over a share is a way of saying the rest isn't really yours either.

title: Five Daily Prayers
objective: After this level you can explain how Muslims prepare for and perform salah five times a day facing Mecca, and why Friday prayer is special.
summary: Muslims pray at dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and evening, after washing, facing the Kaaba in Mecca; on Friday the prayer after noon becomes a congregational prayer with sermons.

cards.headline: Five times a day, Muslims everywhere turn toward one building in Mecca.
cards.body: Which building, and how does a prayer unfold, from the first splash of water to the last bow?

cards.headline: Five set times
cards.body: The day's prayers have names: fajr at dawn, zuhr at midday, asr in the afternoon, maghrib at sunset and isha in the evening. From a raised place in the mosque, often a tower, the muezzin chants the call to prayer aloud. Think of it as a town clock that asks you to stop rather than hurry.

cards.headline: Wash, face, bow
cards.body: First comes wudu, washing the hands, face and feet, which is why mosques have washing facilities. Then the worshipper faces the qibla: the direction of the Kaaba, a cube-shaped shrine in Mecca's Great Mosque. In a mosque, a niche called the mihrab points the way. Each unit of prayer, a rakah, moves through standing, a bow and two prostrations, with "God is great" at every change of posture.

cards.headline: Alone, or shoulder to shoulder
cards.body: Muslims believe each worshipper speaks to God directly in prayer, with no priest in between; the imam who leads a mosque's prayers is not a priest. Muslims can pray anywhere, but praying together in a mosque is especially valued, rows side by side, as a sign that all are equal before God. On Friday the prayer just after noon becomes jumu'ah, a congregational prayer with two sermons from the pulpit.

title: Ramadan and the Two Eids
objective: After this level you can explain why Muslims fast from dawn to sunset in Ramadan and what Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha celebrate.
summary: In Ramadan Muslims fast from dawn to sunset to grow mindful of God; Eid al-Fitr ends the fast, and Eid al-Adha, at the height of the hajj, remembers Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son.

cards.headline: A month without lunch, then one of Islam's two great festivals.
cards.body: Why do Muslims choose to go without food and water all day, and what do they celebrate when it's over?

cards.headline: Dawn to sunset
cards.body: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. From dawn until sunset, Muslims who fast take no food or drink and abstain from sex. Children, the old, the ill, the disabled, travelers on long journeys, and pregnant or nursing women are exempt. Meals bookend the day: suhur before dawn, and after sunset the iftar, which usually begins with dates, as was Muhammad's custom.

cards.headline: Why fast?
cards.body: The Quran says fasting is prescribed so that believers may become mindful of God. Muslims also describe it as training in self-discipline and a way to share the hunger of the poor. It isn't only about food: false words or bad deeds are held to spoil a fast as much as eating. And the month has a birthday. Muslims believe the Quran's revelation began on one of Ramadan's last ten nights in 610, Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power.

mascot.line: People mix up the two Eids. Fitr ends the Ramadan fast; Adha, the sacrifice, comes with the hajj.

cards.headline: Two Eids
cards.body: Eid al-Fitr, the "Feast of Fast-Breaking", ends Ramadan: new clothes for children, prayers at the mosque, gifts and family meals, and thanks to God for the strength to keep the fast. Eid al-Adha, the "Festival of Sacrifice", begins on the 10th of Dhu al-Hijjah, at the height of the hajj. It remembers the story, as Muslims tell it, of Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son Ishmael, who was replaced by a ram. Families sacrifice an animal and share the meat with the poor, relatives and friends.

title: The Hajj
objective: After this level you can describe the rites of the pilgrimage to Mecca and why every pilgrim wears the same simple white garments.
summary: In ihram's simple clothing pilgrims stand as equals, circle the Kaaba, retrace Hagar's search for water, stand at Arafat, stone the pillars at Mina and sacrifice, as Eid al-Adha begins.

cards.headline: Once in a lifetime, if you can manage it.
cards.body: Every adult Muslim who is physically and financially able must make the hajj to Mecca at least once. What happens there, and why does everyone dress alike?

cards.headline: Dressed as equals
cards.body: Before the rites begin, pilgrims enter ihram, a state of ritual purity. Men wrap themselves in two white seamless sheets; women may wear sewn clothes. The hajj is meant to show that everyone is equal before God, and the simple white clothing strips away the markers of status, wealth and pride. Standing in the crowd, you can't tell the rich pilgrim from the poor one.

cards.headline: In Hagar's footsteps
cards.body: In Mecca pilgrims walk around the Kaaba seven times, counterclockwise. Then they walk seven times between two small hills, Safa and Marwa. Muslims believe Hagar ran between them searching for water for her son Ishmael, until the spring of Zamzam gushed from the ground. Today's pilgrims retrace a mother's search.
cards.callout: Tawaf: seven circuits of the Kaaba. Then seven walks between Safa and Marwa

cards.headline: Arafat, stones, sacrifice
cards.body: The hajj runs from the 7th to the 12th of Dhu al-Hijjah. Pilgrims stand praising God in the open on the plain of Arafat, spend the night at Muzdalifah, then throw stones at pillars at Mina that represent the devil. They sacrifice an animal in memory of Abraham's sacrifice; men usually shave their heads and women cut a lock of hair. It is the moment Eid al-Adha begins.

title: Sunni and Shia
objective: After this level you can explain how a dispute over who should lead after Muhammad's death in 632 produced Islam's two main branches.
summary: After 632 most Muslims followed Abu Bakr and the caliphs (Sunnis), while others held that Ali and his descendants should lead (Shia); both share the Quran and the fundamentals of Islam.

cards.headline: One question divided Islam's two main branches: who leads now?
cards.body: When Muhammad died in 632, his followers shared the Quran and the fundamentals of the faith. What they disagreed about was who should lead the community next.

cards.headline: Two answers
cards.body: The larger group chose Abu Bakr, a close Companion of the Prophet, as caliph, and Sunnis recognize the first four caliphs as Muhammad's rightful successors. A smaller group held that leadership belonged to Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and his descendants. The names keep the story. Shia comes from "Shiat Ali", the partisans of Ali. Sunni means one who follows the Sunnah, what the Prophet said and did.

cards.headline: Karbala
cards.body: Ali did become the fourth caliph, but he was killed in 661. In 680 his son Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, was killed with most of his companions at Karbala. Shia Muslims mourn him every year at Ashura. Most Shia, called Twelvers, recognize twelve Imams in Ali's line, the last believed hidden until he returns as the Mahdi.

cards.headline: Two branches, one faith
cards.body: Sunnis and Shia agree on the fundamentals of Islam, share the Quran, and both hold that Muhammad was the final prophet. In 2009 Pew estimated that 87 to 90 percent of the world's Muslims are Sunni and 10 to 13 percent Shia. Shia Muslims are a majority in four countries: Iran, Azerbaijan, Bahrain and Iraq. Level 4's lesson holds here too: one faith, many voices.

title: Hadith and Islamic Law
objective: After this level you can explain how scholars build sharia from the Quran and the Prophet's example, and why schools of law reach different rulings.
summary: Hadith record the Prophet's example; with the Quran, consensus and analogy, jurists use them to work out sharia, and four Sunni schools reach different rulings by different methods.

cards.headline: The Quran comes first. What happens when it doesn't answer the question?
cards.body: They look next to the Prophet's example, recorded in the hadith, and then to scholars' consensus and careful reasoning by analogy. That chain of steps is how Islamic law gets built.

cards.headline: Hadith: the Prophet's example on record
cards.body: A hadith is a report of what Muhammad said or did, and Muslims revere the hadith as a source of law and guidance second only to the Quran. Together they show his Sunnah, the norms and practices he set. Every report carries a chain of narrators, the isnad, running back to Muhammad and his Companions, plus its text. Scholars graded reports as sound, fair or weak.
cards.callout: Isnad = chain of narrators. Matn = the text

cards.headline: Collected and checked
cards.body: Al-Bukhari, who died in 870, and Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, who died in 875, each compiled a collection titled "The Authentic"; both are among the six collections Sunnis hold canonical. Shia Muslims have their own, such as al-Kulayni's Kitab al-kafi. Among the transmitters was Muhammad's wife Aisha, who spent her later years passing on hadith and interpreting the Quran.

mascot.line: People mix up sharia and fiqh. Sharia is the path Muslims believe God set; fiqh is scholars' human attempt to map it.

cards.headline: From sources to rulings
cards.body: Sharia literally means "path leading to the watering place". Fiqh, "understanding", is the human effort to know it, held to be imperfect and changeable where sharia is not. Jurists work from four sources: the Quran, the Sunnah, ijma (scholars' consensus) and qiyas (analogy). Qiyas at work: drugs were ruled forbidden by analogy with the Quran's ban on alcohol, because both intoxicate.

cards.headline: Four schools, one path
cards.body: Sunnis accept four schools of law: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafii and Hanbali. Their methods differ. Malikis and Hanafis gave more weight to their regional traditions, while al-Shafii stressed the Quran, the Sunnah and systematic analogy. The Hanafi school came to predominate in the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent, the Maliki in North, West and Central Africa, the Hanbali in Saudi Arabia. A saying attributed to the Prophet calls difference of opinion "a sign of God's bounty".

title: Hinduism, a Family of Traditions
objective: After this level you can explain why Hinduism has no single founder, creed or central authority, and where the word "Hindu" comes from.
summary: Hinduism has no single founder, scripture or agreed set of teachings, so it is often called a family of religions. Its name comes from Sindhu, the river Indus.

cards.headline: No single founder, no single holy book, no agreed creed. Is it one religion?
cards.body: About 15 percent of the world's people were Hindu in 2020. Yet Hinduism has no founder to point to and no single book everyone must accept. Many writers answer the puzzle by calling it a family. Let's see why, starting with its name.

cards.headline: A family, not a single church
cards.body: Hinduism has no single founder, no single scripture and no commonly agreed set of teachings. Over its long history, many teachers taught different philosophies and wrote many holy books. That's why writers often call it "a way of life" or "a family of religions" rather than one religion. Think of a big family reunion: nobody at the party started the family, yet everyone knows they belong.

cards.headline: A name borrowed from a river
cards.body: The word Hindu comes from Sindhu, the Sanskrit name for the river Indus. Persians, and later Greeks, used the river's name for the land and the people who lived there. So the name began as geography, not theology. The "ism" came much later: British writers coined "Hinduism" in the early 19th century. Many Hindus prefer their own name for their tradition, sanatana dharma, "the eternal law".

cards.headline: What the family shares
cards.body: Hard to define doesn't mean shapeless. Hinduism is rooted in India, which in 2020 was home to 95 percent of the world's Hindus. Most Hindus revere a body of scripture called the Veda. Most draw on a shared set of values called dharma: duty, virtue, the right way to live. Like any family, its members share a home, a library and a way of life, even when their customs differ.

title: The Vedas and Upanishads
objective: After this level you can explain what the Vedas are and the Upanishads' teaching that the self (atman) is one with ultimate reality (Brahman).
summary: Four Vedas, each in four layers, end with the Upanishads. There, teachers ask what the self is, and some answer that atman, the self, is one with Brahman.

cards.headline: The oldest Hindu scriptures grew up around a sacred fire.
cards.body: Priests used one Veda as a handbook for performing sacrifices, and another for the chants sung at them. Then, in the Vedas' final layer, teachers began asking a quieter question: what am I, really?

cards.headline: Four Vedas, four layers
cards.body: There are four Vedas: the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda and Atharvaveda. Each has four layers. The Samhitas are largely hymns praising gods; the Brahmanas mostly explain rituals; then come the Aranyakas and, last, the Upanishads. Some Upanishads turn to life, death and the nature of reality. The oldest are generally dated between 700 and 500 BCE. Coming last, they're also called Vedanta, "the end of the Vedas".

cards.headline: Salt in water
cards.body: In the Chandogya Upanishad, a teacher named Uddalaka gives his son Shvetaketu an odd task: put salt in water and come back tomorrow. The next day the boy can't see the salt anywhere, yet he tastes it throughout the water. The self is like that, Uddalaka says: unseen, yet present throughout. And again and again he tells his son: "you are that" (tat tvam asi).

mascot.line: Keep this pair close: atman, the self; Brahman, the power upholding everything. The next few levels lean on both.

cards.headline: Atman and Brahman
cards.body: Two words carry this teaching. Atman means the eternal self. Brahman is the power that upholds and supports everything. Some Upanishadic teachers, such as Yajnavalkya, say the two are one. Uddalaka himself never uses the word brahman, but the philosopher Shankara later read "you are that" this way: your deepest self and ultimate reality are identical. Not everyone reads it so, which is Level 41's family at work.
