title: Karma, Rebirth and Moksha
objective: After this level you can explain why belief in karma and rebirth makes release (moksha) the highest goal for many Hindus.
summary: Karma means action and its results, carried across lives in samsara. Since every rebirth stays inside the cycle, moksha, release from it, is the final and ultimate aim.

cards.headline: What if this life is one of many, and the goal is to stop coming back?
cards.body: For many Hindus, death is a doorway to another life. That makes the ultimate hope surprising: not a better next life, but freedom from the whole cycle. Here's the logic, one idea at a time.

cards.headline: Karma: every action echoes
cards.body: Karma literally means "action". It names a law: good actions, in harmony with dharma, bring good results, and bad actions bring bad ones. The results may arrive in this life or in a future one. Think of a boomerang: what you throw comes back, sometimes much later.
cards.callout: Karma = action, and what it sets in motion

cards.headline: Samsara: one self, many bodies
cards.body: Remember atman from Level 42? Because the self is understood as eternal, the same being can live in one temporary body after another. This continuous cycle of rebirth is samsara. Many Hindus believe the soul may pass into a human, an animal or even a divine body, according to its karma. Same traveler, new vehicle.

cards.headline: Moksha: stepping off the wheel
cards.body: Hindu texts name three goals of life: virtue (dharma), worldly success and pleasure. A fourth was added later: moksha, liberation from the cycle of action and reaction, and from rebirth itself. Why rank it last and highest? Because the results of karma, Hindus believe, may come even in a heavenly realm, and the self stays there only for a time. The Brahma Sutra calls moksha the ultimate goal.

title: One Divine, Many Forms
objective: After this level you can explain how many Hindus worship Vishnu, Shiva or the Goddess as forms of one ultimate reality.
summary: Most Hindus believe in one Supreme God whose forms are many deities. Each person may choose a form to love, and three great traditions center on Vishnu, Shiva and Devi.

cards.headline: Two neighbors pray at two different shrines, one to Shiva, one to Vishnu.
cards.body: Are they worshipping different gods? Many Hindus would say they are approaching the same Supreme God through different forms. Here's how one and many fit together.

cards.headline: One light, many lamps
cards.body: Outsiders often call Hindus polytheists, yet many Hindus describe themselves as monotheists. Both labels reach for something real. Most Hindus believe in one Supreme God whose qualities and forms are shown in many deities. Many believe all the deities are aspects of one transcendent power, and some see particular deities as forms of Brahman, the power you met in Level 42. Picture a row of lamps lit from a single flame.

cards.headline: Your chosen form
cards.body: Which form do you pray to? Hindu tradition leaves room to choose. Each person can relate to God through a chosen form, the ishta devata, "desired form of God". One person is drawn to Shiva, another to Krishna, another to the goddess Kali. It's a bit like many doors into the same house: you use the one that feels like yours.

cards.headline: Three great traditions
cards.body: Devotion gathered into great traditions that took shape in the Gupta period, 320 to 500 CE. Vaishnavism centers on Vishnu and his avatars, such as Rama and Krishna. Shaivism centers on Shiva. Shaktism centers on Devi, the Goddess. A classic trio, the Trimurti, sums up the divine work: Brahma creates, Vishnu preserves, and Shiva destroys in order to re-create.

title: Three Paths in the Gita
objective: After this level you can explain the paths of action, knowledge and devotion that the Bhagavad Gita teaches.
summary: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna answers Prince Arjuna's crisis with three paths: action without attachment to results, knowledge, and devotion.

cards.headline: A prince freezes before battle. His charioteer's reply became scripture.
cards.body: The Bhagavad Gita, "Song of the Lord", is one of the most popular Hindu texts. It's a conversation that starts with a crisis and ends with three ways to live.

cards.headline: A crisis between two armies
cards.body: The Gita sits inside the sixth book of the Mahabharata. It's a dialogue between Prince Arjuna and Krishna, his charioteer, whom Vaishnavas honor as an avatar of Vishnu. Arjuna faces a war that means killing relatives, friends and teachers, and he wants to withdraw. Krishna's reply fills the text. Hindus class the Gita as smriti, "remembered" tradition, not shruti like the Vedas, yet it ranks among the most popular Hindu texts.

cards.headline: Act, but let go of the results
cards.body: Krishna's first answer is the path of action, karma. Do your duty, he teaches, but act without desire for its results: nishkama karma. You still do the work; you just stop clutching the outcome. Think of planting a tree whose shade you may never sit in.

mascot.line: Keep the trio: action, knowledge, devotion. Three paths, and the Gita points every one of them toward liberation.

cards.headline: Knowledge and devotion
cards.body: Krishna also teaches a path of knowledge, jnana, and a path of devotion, bhakti. In Britannica's reading, devotion is presented as resolving the pull between action and knowledge. Britannica sums up Hinduism's three paths to liberation the same way: action, knowledge and devotion. Three roads toward the moksha of Level 43.

title: Puja and Darshan
objective: After this level you can explain how Hindus worship through puja at home and in temples, and what it means to receive darshan.
summary: Puja ranges from brief rites at a home shrine to temple rituals: offerings, blessed food and care for the sacred image. At its heart is darshan, seeing and being seen.

cards.headline: At a Hindu shrine, you go to see, and to be seen.
cards.body: Hindu worship is mainly a personal act of offering rather than a group service. Here's what happens at a home shrine and in a temple, and why the eyes matter so much.

cards.headline: Puja at home
cards.body: Puja is Hindu ceremonial worship, from brief daily rites at home to elaborate temple rituals. Most Hindu homes have a shrine: a room, a small altar, or simply pictures. There family members offer water, fruit, flowers and incense. Because puja is mainly an individual act, not a communal one, nobody needs to wait for a service to start. Daily worship can begin right at home.

cards.headline: The temple's daily rhythm
cards.body: Wherever it happens, puja has three parts: seeing the deity, making offerings such as flowers, fruit and food, and receiving back the blessed food. In temples, priests perform puja at sunrise, noon, sunset and midnight. The sacred image may be bathed and clothed, the kind of daily care you'd give an honored guest.

cards.headline: Darshan: seeing and being seen
cards.body: The heart of a visit is darshan, "seeing": beholding the deity, especially in its image, or a revered person or sacred object. It works both ways. The worshipper looks, and is blessed by being seen. Pilgrimage runs on the same idea: Hindus travel to rivers, temples and mountains to see and be seen by the deity.

title: Diwali, Holi and the Hindu Year
objective: After this level you can explain the stories and customs behind Diwali and Holi, and why their dates follow the moon.
summary: Diwali lights lamps at the new moon of Kartika; Holi throws colors at the full moon of Phalguna. Both follow lunar months, so their Western dates move each year.

cards.headline: Two festivals, two moons: Diwali at a new moon, Holi at a full moon.
cards.body: Diwali usually lands in October or November, Holi in February or March, but never on the same date twice in a row. Here are their stories, their customs and the calendar that moves them.

cards.headline: Diwali: a row of lights
cards.body: Diwali comes from Sanskrit dipavali, "row of lights". For five days, homes glow with diyas, small earthenware oil lamps, lit to honor Lakshmi, goddess of wealth. In northern India many recall Rama's return to Ayodhya; in the south, Krishna's victory over Narakasura. The legends differ from region to region, but the message is shared: good over evil, light over darkness.

cards.headline: Same lamps, other stories
cards.body: Diwali isn't only Hindu. Jains mark it as the liberation of Mahavira, the most recent of their Tirthankaras. Sikhs mark it as Guru Hargobind's return to Amritsar from captivity. One festival night, three communities, each with its own reason to light a lamp.

cards.headline: Holi: a festival of colors
cards.body: Holi falls on the full moon of Phalguna. Its bonfires recall Prahlada, a devotee of Vishnu, who survived the fire in which his aunt Holika burned: good over evil again. Then come the colors, as people throw colored powder and colored water at one another, and usual social rankings are set aside for a while before order returns. Don't wear your best white shirt.

cards.headline: Why the dates move
cards.body: Both festivals follow the Hindu calendar, which counts 12 lunar months, about 354 days, and adds extra months to keep up with the solar year. A festival tied to a moon, like Diwali's new moon of Kartika, lands on a different Western date each year, but always around the same season.

title: Mahavira and Nonviolence
objective: After this level you can explain how Jainism took shape around Mahavira and why Jains extend nonviolence (ahimsa) to every living thing.
summary: Jains see Mahavira, a prince turned ascetic, as the 24th and last tirthankara of this age. Because every living thing has a soul, harming any of them binds karma.

cards.headline: Would you change the way you walk to avoid stepping on an ant?
cards.body: For many Jains, the answer shapes daily life, because an ant, like every living thing, has a soul. The story starts with a prince who walked away from a palace.

cards.headline: The prince who left
cards.body: Jain tradition tells of Vardhamana, a prince who left the palace at 30 and spent twelve and a half years fasting and meditating until he reached enlightenment. He became Mahavira, "Great Hero". His traditional dates are 599 to 527 BCE, though some modern scholars place him later; he was a contemporary of the Buddha. The two main Jain branches tell some details of his life differently.

cards.headline: Not a founder, a ford builder
cards.body: Jains don't call Mahavira their founder. They believe their teachings are eternal. Mahavira is the 24th and last tirthankara of this age: a "ford builder" who shows others how to cross the currents of life. Such teachers are also called Jinas, "conquerors", because they conquered their own passions. Jains are, quite literally, followers of the conquerors.

cards.headline: A soul in every living thing
cards.body: Why such care for an ant? Jains believe every living thing has a soul, jiva. Even earth, water, fire, air and plants hold beings with one sense, touch; insects like ants have three. And harm has a cost: karma, Jains believe, is a physical substance that sticks to the soul, and harming others attracts much of it. So ahimsa, non-violence, is the heart of Jain teaching: to save your own soul, protect every other one.

title: Jain Vows and Many-Sided Truth
objective: After this level you can explain the five Jain vows, how monks, nuns and laypeople keep them, and the idea that truth has many sides.
summary: Jains keep five vows, fully as monks and nuns, in a lesser form as laypeople. Anekanta teaches that no single view captures the whole truth.

cards.headline: Why would a monk carry a small broom wherever he goes?
cards.body: Not for housework. It's one of the simplest tools of a life built on five vows, and a clue to how Jains think about truth itself.

mascot.line: People mix up the two sets. Great vows (mahavratas): monks and nuns. Lesser vows (anuvratas): laypeople. Same five.

cards.headline: Five vows
cards.body: Jains keep five vows: non-violence (ahimsa), truthfulness (satya), not stealing, sexual restraint, and non-attachment to possessions (aparigraha). Monks and nuns keep them as mahavratas, "great vows". Laypeople keep them as anuvratas, "lesser vows". Same five promises, kept at different depths.

cards.headline: Two ways to keep them
cards.body: A monk sweeps the ground ahead with great care to avoid crushing insects, and some wear a cloth over the mouth. Digambara ("sky clad") monks wear no clothes and own only a whisk broom and a water pot; Svetambara ("white clad") monks and nuns wear white. Full non-violence doesn't fit everyday life, so lay Jains keep the vows in a limited way: eating vegetarian, filtering drinking water, not eating at night, owning only what they need.

cards.headline: The elephant and the blind men
cards.body: A famous Jain parable: several blind men meet an elephant. One feels an ear and says it's a fan. One feels a leg: a post. One feels the side: a wall. Each is partly right, and none has the whole. That's anekanta, "non-one-sidedness": no single view or statement captures the complete truth. Next time you're sure you've got the whole elephant, check which part you're holding.

title: The Buddha's Story
objective: After this level you can retell the traditional story of Siddhartha Gautama's awakening and say what historians can confirm about him.
summary: Tradition tells how Prince Siddhartha Gautama left home at 29 and awakened at Bodh Gaya. Scholars accept that he lived, though his dates and the details of his life are uncertain.

cards.headline: A prince walked out of his palace at 29 and never went back.
cards.body: That is how Buddhists begin the story of Siddhartha Gautama, the man they call the Buddha. Here is the story as the tradition tells it, and then a harder question: what can historians actually confirm?

cards.headline: The prince and the four sights
cards.body: Buddhist tradition says Siddhartha Gautama was born at Lumbini, in today's southern Nepal, into the Shakya clan. That is why he is often called Shakyamuni, "sage of the Shakyas". He grew up in luxury. Then, the traditional accounts say, he saw four sights: an old man, a sick person, a corpse and a monk. Age, sickness and death come even to princes. At 29 he left his comfortable life behind to look for a way through them.

cards.headline: Six hard years, then one night under a tree
cards.body: For six years he lived as an ascetic, practicing harsh self-denial. Then, Buddhists hold, he sat beneath a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya, in northeastern India, and attained enlightenment. From then on he was the Buddha: an awakened one, who has woken from the sleep of ignorance and been freed from suffering. Tradition says he spent the next 45 years teaching across northeastern India and died at Kushinagar at about 80.

mascot.line: Two layers, one life: the story believers tell, and the stone historians can date. Keep both, and keep them apart.

cards.headline: What historians can say
cards.body: Scholars accept that the Buddha lived. But the events in the stories about him can't be taken with confidence as history, and even his dates are uncertain: scholars place his death around 480 BCE or as much as a century later. One early clue is cut in stone. Emperor Ashoka, who ruled from about 273 to 232 BCE, left an inscription recording his visit to the spot he believed was the Buddha's birthplace. Biographies came only centuries later, from around the start of the Common Era.

title: The Four Noble Truths
objective: After this level you can explain the Buddha's diagnosis of suffering, its cause in craving, and why he taught that it can end.
summary: In his first sermon at Sarnath, the Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its cause in craving, its end in nirvana, and the Eightfold Path that leads there.

cards.headline: The Buddha's first sermon fits in four sentences.
cards.body: Buddhists call them the Four Noble Truths. Think of a visit to a doctor: what's wrong, what causes it, whether it can be cured, and the treatment.

cards.headline: Five old companions at a deer park
cards.body: After his enlightenment, the Buddha went to the Deer Park at Sarnath. His audience was five ascetics, his former companions from the years of self-denial. Buddhists call that first sermon setting the wheel of the dharma, the teaching, in motion. At its heart were four truths.

cards.headline: Truth one: nothing fully satisfies
cards.body: The first truth is dukkha, usually translated "suffering". It is wider than pain. Dukkha carries a sense of uneasiness or dissatisfaction, rooted in a world that keeps changing. Think of the best meal of your life: even while you eat it, it is ending. Buddhists see dukkha running through the whole cycle of rebirth, samsara.

cards.headline: Cause, cure, treatment
cards.body: The second truth names the cause: craving (tanha), a thirst that keeps reaching for more. The third says suffering can cease, and its cessation is nirvana. The fourth gives the way there: the Eightfold Path. That is the logic of the whole teaching. If suffering has a cause, removing the cause can end it.

title: The Middle Way
objective: After this level you can explain why the Buddha rejected both luxury and harsh self-denial, and how the Eightfold Path and meditation put the middle way into practice.
summary: The Buddha rejected both luxury and harsh self-denial and taught a middle way: the Eightfold Path of wisdom, ethics and concentration, with meditation at its heart.

cards.headline: Palace or starvation? The Buddha tried both.
cards.body: He grew up in luxury, then spent six years in harsh self-denial. In his first sermon he called both extremes fruitless. What he taught instead became the heart of Buddhist practice.

cards.headline: The middle way
cards.body: In that first sermon, the Buddha described a middle way between two extremes: self-indulgence, and self-mortification, the punishing of your own body. He rejected both as fruitless. He spoke from experience, having lived each one, first as a prince and then as an ascetic. The middle way is not a shrug halfway between. It is a path of its own.

cards.headline: Eight parts, three trainings
cards.body: The middle way has a map: the Eightfold Path. Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration. Buddhist tradition groups them into three trainings. Wisdom: view and intention. Ethics: speech, action and livelihood. Concentration: effort, mindfulness and concentration. Notice how everyday some are: how you talk, how you earn a living.

cards.headline: Sitting still on purpose
cards.body: The third training is where meditation lives. Buddhists practice samatha, calming meditation, and vipassana, insight meditation, learning to watch their own thoughts and feelings with detachment. Mindfulness and concentration aren't extras bolted on: they are two of the path's eight parts.

title: No Self and Nirvana
objective: After this level you can explain why Buddhists teach that nothing is permanent and there is no fixed self, and what nirvana means.
summary: Buddhists teach impermanence, suffering and no-self: a person is five changing factors. Nirvana, the "blowing out" of desire, hatred and ignorance, ends suffering and rebirth.

cards.headline: Are you the same person you were at five?
cards.body: Your body, your moods and your opinions have all changed since then. Buddhist teaching takes that question seriously, and it leads somewhere surprising: to no fixed self at all, and to nirvana.

cards.headline: Three marks of everything
cards.body: Buddhist teaching names three characteristics of all existence. Anicca: impermanence. Dukkha: suffering, Level 52's first truth. And anatta: no-self. Buddhists teach that there is in humans no permanent, underlying substance that can be called a soul. A person is five factors, the skandhas, all constantly changing. Less a stone, more a river.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: nirvana isn't a heaven you travel to. Picture a flame going out, not a door opening.

cards.headline: Blowing out the flame
cards.body: Nirvana literally means "blowing out", the way a flame is blown out. What goes out is desire, hatred and ignorance, and in the end suffering and rebirth themselves. So nirvana is not a place. It is an absence, above all the absence of suffering.

cards.headline: Nirvana in life, and at death
cards.body: Buddhists distinguish two kinds. Nirvana can be reached in this life, while the body carries on. Final nirvana comes at death, when the causes of any future existence have been extinguished. Buddhists hold that the Buddha entered it when he died at Kushinagar, never to be born again.

title: Monks, Nuns and Laypeople
objective: After this level you can explain the Three Jewels and why monastics and lay Buddhists depend on each other, from the alms round to Vesak.
summary: Buddhists take refuge in the Three Jewels: the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha. Monks, nuns and laypeople depend on each other, from the dawn alms round to Vesak, the festival of the Buddha's life.

cards.headline: Before dawn in Thailand, monks set out barefoot, each carrying a bowl.
cards.body: They will eat what people place in those bowls. Nobody pays, and nobody buys. What's going on is one of Buddhism's oldest partnerships.

cards.headline: Three Jewels
cards.body: What makes someone a Buddhist? Traditionally, three short sentences: "I go to the Buddha for refuge, I go to the Doctrine for refuge, I go to the Order for refuge." Saying them is how a person becomes a Buddhist. They name the Three Jewels: the Buddha, the dharma (his teaching) and the sangha (the community).

cards.headline: A community of four
cards.body: The sangha has traditionally had four groups: monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen. It began with the five ascetics of the first sermon, who became the first monks. Then, at the request of his stepmother Mahaprajapati and other women, the Buddha also established an order of nuns.

cards.headline: Food one way, blessing the other
cards.body: The order depends on laypeople for its support, from alms to gifts of money and land. In Thailand, monastic rules bar monks from farming, and they eat what is offered in their bowls. The exchange runs both ways: the monk blesses the food, and the giver gains merit. Every morning, the bowl ties the two halves of the community together.

cards.headline: Vesak: one full moon, three events
cards.body: Once a year comes Vesak, marking the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death. It falls on the full-moon day of the month Vesakha, in April, May or June. Laypeople bring flowers or light incense at temples, and make merit through good deeds.

title: Three Schools of Buddhism
objective: After this level you can compare Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism, why they differ and where each is practiced.
summary: Theravada keeps the Pali canon and the arhat ideal; Mahayana, in East Asia, honors the bodhisattva; Vajrayana, notably in Tibet, adds mantras and mandalas.

cards.headline: Visit a temple in Thailand, then Japan, then Tibet.
cards.body: All three are Buddhist, yet each belongs to a different school, with its own scripture, ideal or practice. Here are the three great schools, and what makes each distinct.

cards.headline: Theravada: the Way of the Elders
cards.body: Theravada means "Way of the Elders". It predominates in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos, and its scripture is the Pali canon, first written down in Sri Lanka (Level 6). Its ideal is the arhat: a perfected saint who reaches enlightenment through their own effort. Traditionally, that path runs through monastic life.

cards.headline: Mahayana: the Greater Vehicle
cards.body: Mahayana, the "Greater Vehicle", arose within Indian Buddhism around the beginning of the Common Era and predominates in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam. Its ideal is the bodhisattva, who vows to reach enlightenment but delays entering nirvana to help all other beings reach liberation. And anyone, Mahayana teaches, can become a bodhisattva, not only monks.
cards.callout: Arhat: awakening by your own effort. Bodhisattva: awakening for all.

cards.headline: Vajrayana: the Diamond Vehicle
cards.body: Vajrayana, the "Thunderbolt" or "Diamond Vehicle", developed later within Mahayana, in India and neighboring lands, above all Tibet. It adds powerful tools for meditation: mantras, sacred sounds that keep the mind from straying, and mandalas, representations of the universe used as aids to meditation.

title: Guru Nanak and the Ten Gurus
objective: After this level you can explain why Guru Nanak's message of one God and equality began a new faith in Punjab around 1500.
summary: Guru Nanak, born in 1469, taught one God, honest work and sharing, declaring "There is no Hindu; there is no Muslim." His langar seated everyone as equals, and nine Gurus followed him.

cards.headline: A man vanished while bathing in a river. Three days later he came back.
cards.body: What he said next is remembered by Sikhs as the start of Guru Nanak's mission, and of a new faith in Punjab.

cards.headline: The words at the river
cards.body: Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan. According to Sikh tradition, at about 30 he disappeared while bathing in a river. Three days later he returned and declared: "There is no Hindu; there is no Muslim." It is a sentence that looks past religious labels to the people underneath.

cards.headline: One God, honest work, sharing
cards.body: Sikhs believe in one God. Nanak taught three things you can do every day: remember God's Name, earn an honest living and share with others. After years of travel he settled at Kartarpur, where the first Sikh community took shape. His followers were Sikhs, from the Punjabi word for "learner".
cards.callout: Remember God's Name, work honestly, share

cards.headline: Everyone sits in one line
cards.body: Equality has a very practical form: the langar, the free kitchen of the gurdwara. It serves vegetarian food to everyone, whatever their background. And everyone sits in one straight line, neither ahead to claim higher status nor behind to show a lower one. In a society divided by caste, the langar began as a protest against that division.

cards.headline: Ten Gurus, one spirit
cards.body: Before his death in 1539, Nanak named a successor, Guru Angad. That began a line of ten human Gurus, ending with Guru Gobind Singh in 1708. Sikhs believe all ten were inhabited by a single spirit, so each carried the same message forward.

title: The Guru Granth Sahib
objective: After this level you can explain why Sikhs treat their scripture as a living Guru, and what happens in a gurdwara.
summary: Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth in 1604. After Guru Gobind Singh's death in 1708 the scripture became the Guru Granth Sahib, the living Guru at the heart of every gurdwara.

cards.headline: Sikhs have a Guru today. It is a book.
cards.body: Each morning in a gurdwara it is ceremonially opened, and each night it is wrapped and put away. Why would a community treat a scripture the way you would treat a revered teacher?

cards.headline: Compiled in 1604
cards.body: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, compiled the first version, the Adi Granth ("First Book"), at Amritsar in 1604. He gathered his own hymns and those of the Gurus before him, and added devotional songs by Hindu and Muslim saints, notably the poet Kabir. Today's printed edition runs to 1,430 pages, its hymns arranged by the ragas, the musical modes in which they are sung.

mascot.line: Keep this: since 1708, the Guru for Sikhs is the scripture itself. Everything in a gurdwara follows from that.

cards.headline: From ten Gurus to one
cards.body: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, declared an end to the line of human Gurus. After his death in 1708, the scripture took the Guru's place as the Guru Granth Sahib. Spiritual authority now rests in the book, while the community, the Panth, handles worldly matters. That is why Sikhs treat it as a living Guru, not just a text about one.

cards.headline: Inside a gurdwara
cards.body: Gurdwara means "doorway to the Guru". Inside, the Guru Granth Sahib rests on a cot under a canopy, opened in the morning and wrapped and put away at night. Services bring scripture recitation and hymns sung with instruments, and the doors are open to all. Most gurdwaras also have a langar, so the hymns lead to a shared meal.

title: The Khalsa and the Five Ks
objective: After this level you can explain why Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699 and what the Five Ks mean to Sikhs who wear them.
summary: After his father's execution in 1675, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699: a casteless order of initiated Sikhs who take the names Singh and Kaur and wear the Five Ks as articles of faith.

cards.headline: A plain steel bracelet can be a promise.
cards.body: For initiated Sikhs, the kara is one of five articles of faith worn every day. All five go back to Baisakhi Day in 1699.

cards.headline: A Guru in hard times
cards.body: Gobind Singh became the tenth Guru in 1675, at nine, after his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, was executed by the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. On Baisakhi Day in 1699, at Anandpur in Punjab, he founded the Khalsa: a casteless order of Sikhs committed to courage and to their faith. Those who join are initiated with amrit, sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword.

cards.headline: Shared names
cards.body: Khalsa men take the name Singh, "lion", and women the name Kaur, "princess". Members also pledge to give up tobacco, alcohol and certain meats. One surname for every man, one for every woman: a casteless order, written into people's names.

cards.headline: The Five Ks
cards.body: Initiated Khalsa Sikhs wear five articles of faith, each beginning with K. Kesh: uncut hair, for belonging. Kara: a steel bracelet, for self-restraint and discipline. Kangha: a comb, for cleanliness. Kirpan: a sword, for self-respect and readiness to face challenges. Kachera: an undergarment, for moral restraint.

title: Honoring the Ancestors
objective: After this level you can explain Chinese ancestor veneration and why families sweep graves at the Qingming festival.
summary: Chinese families have honored their ancestors since the Neolithic, with name tablets and incense at the home altar. At Qingming in early April, that care goes out to the grave.

cards.headline: Each spring, Chinese families go out to sweep their ancestors' tombs. Why?
cards.body: The festival is called Qingming. To understand it, don't start at the grave. Start at home, where the ancestors have a place every day.

cards.headline: The ancestors have a place at home
cards.body: Honoring ancestors in China is very old: it was deeply rooted by the Late Neolithic. Traditionally, the head of a household made sure offerings to the family's dead were constantly renewed. On the home altar, wooden tablets carry each ancestor's name with birth and death dates, and incense is offered there morning and evening. Picture a family tree you light incense for, twice a day.

cards.headline: A relationship that runs both ways
cards.body: Why keep it up, day after day? Ancestral spirits are believed to have the power to influence the lives of the living. Offerings honor them, and they are meant to turn away misfortune and bring good fortune. So veneration is more than remembering. It's a relationship: the family cares for its dead, and many believe the dead look after the family.

cards.headline: Clear and Bright
cards.body: Qingming means "Clear and Bright". It falls on the 15th day after the spring equinox, generally in early April, and is sometimes called Tomb Sweeping Day. Families clean their ancestors' tombs and leave offerings, burning incense, spirit money and paper models of valuable goods. The care the home altar gets every day, the grave gets once a year.

title: Confucian Ritual and Family
objective: After this level you can explain Confucian rites and filial piety, and why scholars disagree over whether Confucianism is a religion.
summary: Confucian li asks people to play every role properly, starting with filial piety toward parents in life and after death. Scholars still debate whether this 'diffused' tradition is a religion.

cards.headline: Every September 28, a Taipei temple honors Confucius's birthday.
cards.body: Student musicians play, and the rites unfold in careful order. Is this religion? Before choosing a label, look at what Confucian ritual asks of people.

cards.headline: Li: playing every role properly
cards.body: Confucius traditionally lived from 551 to 479 BCE. At the center of his teaching is li: ritual, etiquette and social convention, and a willingness to play every one of your roles properly. The Analects put it strongly: don't look, listen, speak or move except in accordance with the rites. Think of li as the choreography of a good life.

cards.headline: Filial piety, in life and after
cards.body: Li begins at home. Filial piety, xiao, means serving your parents with proper ritual while they live, then burying them and sacrificing to them properly after death. Ancestral sacrifice showed reverence and asked the ancestors' spirits to help and protect the living. Level 61's home altar is filial piety that never clocks out.

cards.headline: Rites at the temple
cards.body: Before 1911, China's imperial state rituals included sacrifices at the Confucian temple. The rites continue. The Taipei ceremony has three sections: welcoming Confucius's spirit, paying respects, and escorting the spirit away. Taiwan also keeps September 28 as Teachers' Day: a bow to the first teacher, and to all the others.

mascot.line: People mix up "no separate clergy" with "no religion". Adler's word for this is diffused: woven into family and state.

cards.headline: Religion or not?
cards.body: For most of the 20th century the predominant scholarly view was that Confucianism wasn't "really" a religion, at least not like familiar Western traditions. Most North American scholars of Confucianism now see its religious side as evident, though the wider field still disagrees. Following C. K. Yang, Joseph Adler calls it a "diffused" religion: lived in family, community and state, not in a separate institution run by clergy.

title: Daoism as a Religion
objective: After this level you can explain Daoist temples, priests and rituals, and the Daoist aims of harmony with the Dao and long life.
summary: Daoists date their organized religion to a revelation in 142 CE. Priests with families and celibate monks lead rituals like the jiao, aiming at long life and union with the Dao.

cards.headline: Priests chant in the temple while a parade winds through the streets.
cards.body: It's a Daoist Offering, one of the religion's great rituals. Who are the priests, and what are they working toward?

cards.headline: A revelation in 142 CE
cards.body: Daoists trace their organized religion to a revelation. By tradition, in 142 CE Laozi, worshipped as Lord Lao, appeared to Zhang Daoling and founded the Way of the Celestial Masters. The founding story comes first; the priests and rituals follow.

cards.headline: Priests with families, monks in abbeys
cards.body: The main leader of Daoist ritual is the daoshi, "Daoist master", a role typically passed down within families. Celestial Masters priests marry and live with their families. Quanzhen, found mainly in northern China, is a celibate order of monks and nuns; its White Cloud Abbey in Beijing is the seat of the China Daoist Association. Two ways to serve, one tradition.

cards.headline: The Offering
cards.body: The Offering, jiao, renews the bond between a community and its gods. It usually lasts one to ten days. Inside the temple, priests perform the ritual; outside, a street festival carries the local god's statue through the neighborhood. Another ritual, Merit (gongde), is a funeral rite. Temple and street work as one.

cards.headline: Long life and the Dao
cards.body: What is it all for? "Long life" and "immortality" are among the most recurrent words in Daoist writing, and liberation is often pictured as union with the Dao. Immortals are said to be people who went beyond the limits of ordinary human life, usually through their practices. Quanzhen monks practice meditation and Internal Alchemy (neidan).

title: Buddhism Comes to China
objective: After this level you can explain how Buddhism changed in China into Chan (Zen) and Pure Land, and how the "three teachings" came to share one household.
summary: Buddhism reached China with merchants in the late Han, adapted to family values, and grew Chan (Zen) and Pure Land. Beside Confucianism and Daoism it became one of the 'three teachings'.

cards.headline: "Buddhism is the sun, Daoism the moon, Confucianism the five planets."
cards.body: A 6th-century Chinese scholar wrote that. How did a teaching from outside China come to share its sky?

cards.headline: Arriving with merchants
cards.body: Buddhism began to enter China as a religion of foreign merchants in the later years of the Han dynasty. Early translators rendered "sutra" as jing, the word already used for the Confucian and Daoist classics. A borrowed word was a kind of welcome: Buddhist texts arrived sounding like classics.

cards.headline: Monks in a family culture
cards.body: To some in China, celibate monks and nuns seemed to threaten family values. Buddhism made room for the family. Monastics used kinship terms for one another, and monks and lay donors held rituals to comfort the ancestors. Level 62's filial piety didn't shut Buddhism out; it changed how Buddhism was lived.

cards.headline: Meditation and a name
cards.body: In China two schools took shape. Chan means "Meditation", from the Sanskrit dhyana; in Japanese it's Zen. It calls itself "a special transmission outside the scriptures", pointing straight at the mind. Pure Land devotees call on the name of Amitabha Buddha, hoping to be reborn in his Western Paradise, the Pure Land. One sits in silence; the other calls a name.

cards.headline: Three teachings, one household
cards.body: The Chinese came to speak of sanjiao, the "three teachings": Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism. Li Shiqian's sun, moon and planets put all three in one sky. Remember Level 2's Confucian scholar at a Daoist or Buddhist ritual? Following one tradition didn't demand total commitment to it alone.

title: Shinto and the Kami
objective: After this level you can explain what kami are and how a Shinto shrine marks off sacred space.
summary: Shinto, 'the way of the kami', honors the sacred life-force in nature, ancestors and revered people. A torii marks the border of a shrine, the seat of the kami.

cards.headline: In Japan, a simple gate marks where the everyday world ends.
cards.body: It's a torii, and many people bow slightly before passing through. What lies beyond it?

cards.headline: The way of the kami
cards.body: Shinto literally means "the way of the kami". The Association of Shinto Shrines describes kami as the divine energy or life-force of the natural world: there are kami of rain, wind, mountains, sea and thunder. Kami also include ancestors, and people who gave great service to state or society may be enshrined as kami. The Association adds that Shinto has no founder, no dogma and no doctrine.

cards.headline: A mountain can be a kami
cards.body: Sacred mountains such as Mount Fuji are regarded as kami themselves and as dwelling places of kami. Almost every shrine has a sacred forest, sometimes a single tree, and especially sacred trees are marked with a straw rope, shimenawa. Level 3 put Mount Fuji under Smart's material dimension. Here the place isn't a backdrop. It can be the sacred itself.

mascot.line: Keep this one: a torii marks a border. Outside, the everyday world; inside, the space of the kami.

cards.headline: Inside the gate
cards.body: A shrine, jinja, is the seat of one or more kami. The torii marks its entrance, the border between sacred space and the everyday world. Deepest inside is the place where the kami is present, the most sacred spot of all; often visitors may not enter it, or even see it. At Ise Jingu the main sanctuaries are rebuilt every 20 years, and the kami is moved to the new buildings.

title: Purity, Festivals and Two Faiths
objective: After this level you can explain Shinto purification and festivals, and why many Japanese take part in both Shinto and Buddhist rites.
summary: Shinto prizes purity, from rinsing at the font to twice-yearly Oharae, and thanks the kami in festivals. Shrines mark early life while funerals are mostly Buddhist: two faiths in one life.

cards.headline: In Japan, a baby often visits a Shinto shrine. Funerals are usually Buddhist.
cards.body: Babies are often brought to a shrine about a month after birth. Yet about 90% of funerals, one survey found, are Buddhist. Why would one life pass through two religions? Start with water.

cards.headline: Clean before you enter
cards.body: Purity is very important in Shinto. Most shrines have a water font where visitors rinse their hands and mouth before paying respects. At the ends of June and December many shrines hold Oharae ceremonies to clear away impurities built up over the past six months. In Shinto myth, even Amaterasu, the most revered kami, was born when her father Izanagi cleansed himself after returning from the land of the dead.

cards.headline: Festivals: the kami go out
cards.body: Matsuri, festivals, offer thanks to the kami and pray for the community's happiness, health and prosperity. At many, the kami is moved into a portable shrine, a mikoshi, and carried through the neighborhood. The Niinamesai in November gives thanks for the rice harvest; the day is now a national holiday, Labor Thanksgiving Day.

cards.headline: Beginnings at the shrine, endings at the temple
cards.body: Shrines mark life's beginnings: babies are often brought about a month after birth, and young children at Shichigosan, "seven-five-three". Funerals are not normally held at shrines, because death is regarded as a source of ritual impurity. In one national survey, about 90% of Japanese funerals were Buddhist.

cards.headline: Two faiths, one life
cards.body: The pairing is old. By the late 8th century, kami were thought to be avatars of buddhas, and this combined practice lasted until the Meiji Restoration of 1868. It is still lived: in Pew's 2023 survey, 44% of Japanese Buddhists said they pray or offer respects to kami. For many, it's not either-or.

title: Native American Traditions
objective: After this level you can explain what many Native American traditions share and why each nation's sacred ways belong to that nation.
summary: Many Native American traditions tie the sacred to relationships, oral memory and particular places, like the Diné's four mountains or Bear Lodge. Each nation's sacred ways remain its own.

cards.headline: Every June, climbers are asked to stay off a tower of rock in Wyoming.
cards.body: Many call it Bear Lodge, and more than two dozen tribes are associated with it. June is a time when many of their ceremonies take place.

cards.headline: Threads many traditions share
cards.body: Level 8 warned that there is no single "Native American religion"; practices differ between peoples. Still, some threads run through many of them. Britannica describes religion here as the relationship between living humans and other persons or beings, however they are conceived. Traditional knowledge, passed on orally, keeps the memory of a place's visible and invisible inhabitants.

cards.headline: Four mountains, one homeland
cards.body: For the Diné (Navajo), four sacred mountains surround Dinétah, the Diné homeland: Blanca Peak in the east, Mount Taylor in the south, the San Francisco Peaks in the west and Hesperus Mountain in the north. They are sites of many events in Diné sacred stories, and can be seen as a hogan, a Diné dwelling, that holds the Diné universe.

cards.headline: One tower, many stories
cards.body: The Arapaho, Crow, Cheyenne, Shoshone and Lakota are among the tribes associated with Devils Tower. Most tribes that lived in or near the Black Hills have their own oral histories of how it was created. Because June is culturally significant, the park asks climbers to stay off voluntarily that month. One rock, many nations, many stories.

cards.headline: Sacred ways belong to their nation
cards.body: Access to some sacred knowledge is restricted: some is considered so powerful that instruction and initiation are required. In 1978 the American Indian Religious Freedom Act made it US policy to protect Native peoples' right to believe, express and exercise their traditional religions, including access to sacred sites.

title: The Dreaming and Country
objective: After this level you can explain what the Dreaming means for Aboriginal Australians and why land (Country) is sacred.
summary: The Dreaming, an English name for concepts like Jukurrpa and Tjukurpa, tells of Ancestral Beings who shaped the land and its law. Country, alive and related to its people, is sacred.

cards.headline: Anangu hold Uluru sacred. Their law did not generally permit climbing it.
cards.body: That law is called Tjukurpa. To see why a rock can be sacred, you need two ideas: the Dreaming, and Country.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: the Dreaming isn't sleep, and it isn't only long ago. "Everywhen" is the word to keep.

cards.headline: Not a dream, and not only the past
cards.body: "The Dreaming" is an English translation of a First Nations concept with different names in different languages, such as Jukurrpa in Warlpiri. Older writing called it the "dream-time". Dreaming stories tell of Ancestral Beings who created animals, plants and land formations as they moved through the land, and who set out rules for living. The anthropologist W. E. H. Stanner said it can't be fixed in time: it "was, and is, everywhen".

cards.headline: Tjukurpa at Uluru
cards.body: At Uluru, Anangu speak of Tjukurpa. They describe it as the religious philosophy linking them to the environment and their ancestors, and as their traditional law. It isn't written down. It is memorised and passed on to the right people, like an inheritance.

cards.headline: Country is alive
cards.body: First Nations people use Country for the lands, waters and skies they are connected to through ancestral ties. There are hundreds of Countries, each with its own culture, language and Law. Country is spoken of like a person, alive, and bound to its people by relationship and reciprocity: "We are Country and Country is us."

cards.headline: A religion? Two First Nations answers
cards.body: Anangu say that, like religions elsewhere in the world, Tjukurpa provides answers to many important questions. Common Ground, a First Nations-led organization, puts it differently: the Dreaming is not a religion, and the Ancestral Beings are not gods. Both answers come from First Nations voices.

title: Yoruba Religion and the Orisha
objective: After this level you can explain how Yoruba tradition links a supreme God, the orisha and the ancestors, and what Ifa divination is.
summary: In Yoruba religion the Creator Olorun oversees hundreds of orisha, some of them deified ancestors, while Egungun festivals bring ancestors back. Ifa priests read signs linked to 256 odu.

cards.headline: 256 parts, with hundreds of verses each, chanted by Yoruba priests.
cards.body: That's the store of wisdom behind Ifa divination. First, meet the Creator, the orisha and the ancestors it belongs with.

cards.headline: One Creator, many orisha
cards.body: The Yoruba live mainly in southwestern Nigeria, with smaller groups in Benin and northern Togo. Many are now Christians or Muslims, but aspects of the traditional religion survive. In it, the Almighty Creator, Olorun, oversees the orisha, some 400 lesser gods and spirits. Devotion to the orisha is active and widespread, but Olorun has neither priests nor cult groups.

cards.headline: Three kinds of orisha
cards.body: Orisha fall into three overlapping kinds: primordial divinities, deified ancestors such as kings and city founders, and personified forces of nature. Shango is two at once: an early king of Oyo and a force of fire and lightning. Devotees turn to particular orisha for particular occupations, skills and problems.

cards.headline: The ancestors return
cards.body: Egungun masquerades, often performed at yearly festivals, honor the ancestors and seek blessings for the community. The costume, with gloves, foot covers and a mesh face screen, covers the performer and turns the wearer into a returned ancestor. At Qingming, families visit their ancestors. At Egungun, the ancestors visit.

cards.headline: Ifa: reading the signs
cards.body: The Yoruba regard Ifa, also called Orunmila, as the deity of wisdom. Ifa divination relies not on anyone's oracular powers but on signs read by a priest, the babalawo, with sacred palm nuts and a divination chain. Ifa's 256 odu each hold many verses, about 800, which the priests chant. Ifa is consulted when an important decision has to be made.

title: The Baha'i Faith
objective: After this level you can explain the Baha'i teachings of the oneness of God, religion and humanity, and the faith's beginnings in 1800s Iran.
summary: The Baha'i Faith grew from the Bab's movement in 1844 Iran; Baha'u'llah declared his mission in 1863. Baha'is teach the oneness of God, religion and humanity, with no clergy.

cards.headline: A faith born in 1800s Iran sees one God behind many prophets.
cards.body: Baha'is honor Abraham, Moses, the Buddha, Jesus and Muhammad as messengers of the same God. Here is how their faith began, and the idea at its heart.

cards.headline: Two declarations
cards.body: In 1844, in Shiraz, Iran, a man known as the Bab founded the movement the Baha'i Faith grew out of. One of his followers, Baha'u'llah, was born in Tehran in 1817. In 1852, when the Babis were persecuted, he was thrown into a Tehran dungeon. In 1863 he declared to his fellow Babis that he was the messenger of God the Bab had foretold. He spent the rest of his life in exile in Ottoman lands and died near Akka in 1892.

cards.headline: One God, one religion, one humanity
cards.body: Baha'is sum up their teaching as three onenesses: of God, of religion and of humanity. In their view, God has sent a series of Messengers, among them Abraham, Krishna, Zoroaster, Moses, the Buddha, Jesus and Muhammad, and most recently the Bab and Baha'u'llah. Each, Baha'is believe, brought guidance suited to humanity's stage of growth. They call this progressive revelation. Picture one school with many grades, rather than rival schools.
cards.callout: Oneness of God, of religion, of humanity

cards.headline: No clergy, open doors
cards.body: The Baha'i Faith has no priesthood. Its highest governing body, the Universal House of Justice, is elected. Its Houses of Worship are open to people of every faith or none. The one in New Delhi, the Lotus Temple, opened in 1986: 27 white marble petals, grouped in threes to form nine sides. And in Level 9's world count? Baha'is sit in the small "other religions" group, about 2% of the world together.

title: African Faiths in the Americas
objective: After this level you can explain how Vodou, Santería and Candomblé grew from West African traditions among enslaved people and their descendants.
summary: Vodou in Haiti, Santería in Cuba and Candomblé in Brazil grew from West African traditions among enslaved Africans and their descendants, often honoring the spirits behind Catholic saints.

cards.headline: Three faiths were built by enslaved Africans and their descendants.
cards.body: Vodou in Haiti, Santería in Cuba, Candomblé in Brazil. Each grew from West African traditions in a new land, blended with Catholic elements. How did their spirits and gods endure?

cards.headline: Vodou: God and the lwa
cards.body: The word Vodou means "spirit" or "deity" in Fon, the language of the old kingdom of Dahomey, now Benin. The religion took shape in colonial Saint-Domingue, today's Haiti, among enslaved Dahomean, Kongo, Yoruba and other peoples. In Vodou, God is the "great master", who leaves earthly matters to the lwa: spirits honored in temples led by priestesses, manbo, and priests, oungan.

mascot.line: Keep this: one image, two meanings. A saint's picture could honor an orisha, and that's how worship carried on under cover.

cards.headline: Orishas behind the saints
cards.body: In Cuba, Yoruba people enslaved in great numbers in the early 1800s brought the religion best known as Santería; many practitioners call it Lukumí or Regla de Ocha. The name Santería comes from links some devotees drew between the Yoruba orishas and Catholic saints, santos. In Brazil, Candomblé devotees who could not worship openly did something similar, outwardly equating the orixás with Catholic saints.

cards.headline: Led by women, carried north
cards.body: Candomblé is strongest in the Brazilian state of Bahia, where enslaved Africans and their descendants created it. Most of its devotees are women, and some terreiros, its ritual communities, have long consecrated only women as their supreme leaders. Santería traveled too: from Cuba's 1959 revolution on, nearly one million Cubans left the island, bringing orisha religion to cities such as Miami and New York.

summary: Rastafari began in 1930s Jamaica after Haile Selassie I, once Ras Tafari, was crowned in Ethiopia. Rastas speak of exile in Babylon and home in Zion, with dreadlocks, ital food and drumming.

cards.headline: In 1930 an emperor was crowned in Ethiopia. In Jamaica, a faith was born.
cards.body: Rastafari even takes its name from him. Why would a coronation across an ocean start a new religious movement?

cards.headline: The emperor's old name
cards.body: Haile Selassie I was crowned emperor of Ethiopia in 1930. Before that, his name was Ras Tafari, and the movement that began in Jamaica in the 1930s took that name. Many Rastas regard Haile Selassie as the messiah, the Second Coming of Christ, who came to redeem Black people.

cards.headline: Babylon and Zion
cards.body: Rastas read the Bible's story of exile as their own. People of African descent, Rastas believe, are exiles in Babylon, tested by Jah, their name for God, through slavery and economic injustice. Zion is Ethiopia, the ultimate home of all Africans. An old story of captivity becomes a map home.

cards.headline: A faith you can see and hear
cards.body: Rastafari never formed one central church; its groups share core beliefs without a single headquarters. Its practices are easy to spot: dreadlocks, an "ital" diet that is natural and vegetarian, ganja smoked for meditation, and all-night drumming ceremonies.

title: Church and State in America
objective: After this level you can explain the First Amendment's two religion clauses and where the idea of a "wall of separation" came from.
summary: Virginia's 1786 statute, the First Amendment's Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses and Article VI set out religious freedom; Jefferson's 1802 letter coined the 'wall of separation'.

cards.headline: America's "wall of separation" isn't written in the Constitution.
cards.body: The famous phrase comes from a president's letter to a group of Baptists. Before the letter, though, come the laws it was describing.

cards.headline: Virginia goes first
cards.body: On January 16, 1786, Virginia enacted its Statute for Religious Freedom. Thomas Jefferson wrote it, and James Madison guided it to passage while Jefferson was abroad. It declared that no one could be compelled to support any religious worship, or suffer for their religious opinions or belief. Jefferson was proud of it: he had his authorship listed on his tombstone.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. One clause keeps government from backing a faith; the other keeps it from blocking one.

cards.headline: Two clauses, one sentence
cards.body: The First Amendment, ratified in 1791, begins: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." That holds two clauses. The Establishment Clause bars government from establishing a religion; the Free Exercise Clause protects religious practice. Article VI adds that "no religious Test shall ever be required" for federal office.
cards.callout: Establishment: no official faith. Free exercise: freedom to practice.

cards.headline: The wall
cards.body: The Danbury Baptist Association of Connecticut wrote to President Jefferson, complaining of religious oppression by their state government. On January 1, 1802, he replied that religion "lies solely between Man & his God", and that the First Amendment built "a wall of separation between Church & State." The idea still echoes. In 1976 the Census Bureau's director said a mandatory religion question would appear to infringe on that separation.

title: The Great Awakenings
objective: After this level you can explain how revivals in the 1700s and 1800s reshaped American religion and grew the Baptists and Methodists.
summary: The Great Awakening (about 1720 to the 1740s) and the Second Great Awakening (about 1795 to 1835) called for a 'new birth', invented the camp meeting and grew the Baptists and Methodists.

cards.headline: Picture families camping for days in a Kentucky clearing to hear preaching.
cards.body: That was a camp meeting, the signature of America's revivals. Two great waves of revival reshaped the country's churches. Here's how.

cards.headline: The first wave
cards.body: The Great Awakening swept the British American colonies mainly between about 1720 and the 1740s. In 1739 and 1740 George Whitefield, an Anglican priest, preached up and down the colonies to vast crowds, while Jonathan Edwards became the revival's great thinker and defender. Preachers stressed God's unmerited grace and the "new birth" in Jesus Christ: faith as a turning point you feel.

cards.headline: The second wave
cards.body: A Second Great Awakening followed, from about 1795 to 1835. Its great invention was the camp meeting: families loaded their wagons, pitched tents and stayed for several days. In the summer of 1801 Barton Stone organized a powerful revival at Cane Ridge, near Lexington, Kentucky. The Kentucky revivals stirred intense emotion.

cards.headline: Who grew
cards.body: Revivals helped make the teachings of the Baptists and Methodists accessible to a wider cross section of people. In the second wave many churches grew, above all Methodist and Baptist ones. The revival also stirred reforms, including temperance and the emancipation of women.

title: The Latter-day Saints
objective: After this level you can explain the origins and core beliefs of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and its trek to Utah.
summary: Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon and organized the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in 1830. After his killing in 1844, Brigham Young led the Saints to Utah.

cards.headline: In 1830 a young New Yorker published a book his followers read as scripture.
cards.body: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints reads it beside the Bible. Here is how the church began, and why its members crossed half a continent.

cards.headline: A vision and the plates
cards.body: Joseph Smith grew up in Palmyra, New York. He reported that in 1820, at age 14, God the Father and Jesus Christ appeared to him, and that in 1823 an angel named Moroni told him of golden plates. He published the Book of Mormon in March 1830, and on April 6, 1830, he organized a church.

cards.headline: Another witness
cards.body: Latter-day Saints believe Smith translated the plates "by the gift and power of God". The Church teaches that the Book of Mormon is another witness of Jesus Christ, one that supports the Bible rather than replacing it. Members also hold to continuing revelation, and they emphasize temple worship and missionary work.

cards.headline: West to the beehive
cards.body: The Saints moved from New York to Ohio, Missouri and Illinois, where they built Nauvoo. On June 27, 1844, a mob shot Joseph Smith and his brother Hyrum in jail at Carthage, Illinois. Brigham Young then led a 1,100-mile migration, and the first company entered the Salt Lake Valley in July 1847. Settlers called the region Deseret, a Book of Mormon word for honeybee, and the beehive became Utah's symbol of industry.

title: Adventists, Witnesses, Pentecostals
objective: After this level you can explain how the Seventh-day Adventists, Jehovah's Witnesses and Pentecostals began in America and what sets each apart.
summary: Seventh-day Adventists grew from the Great Disappointment of 1844, Jehovah's Witnesses from Russell's Bible Students, and Pentecostals from the 1906 Azusa Street revival.

cards.headline: Three American-born movements, three distinct paths.
cards.body: One keeps a Saturday Sabbath. One goes door to door. One prays in tongues. Here's where each began.

cards.headline: The day that didn't come
cards.body: William Miller predicted Christ's Second Coming for 1843, then 1844. When it didn't come, most of his followers left, and the letdown became known as the Great Disappointment. A small group kept the hope, came to believe that Saturday, not Sunday, is the Sabbath God commanded, and organized the Seventh-day Adventist Church at Battle Creek, Michigan, in 1863. Ellen G. White, who reported visions, shaped it for decades.

cards.headline: Bible students at the door
cards.body: In 1872 Charles Taze Russell founded a Bible Students movement in Pittsburgh. In 1931 it took the name Jehovah's Witnesses, from the conviction that Jehovah is God's name. Witnesses see Jesus as God's agent rather than part of a Trinity, expect a coming kingdom on earth, and are known for preaching door to door, which they call witnessing.

mascot.line: Easy to blur these three. Adventists began with a date, Witnesses with Bible study, Pentecostals with a revival.

cards.headline: Fire on Azusa Street
cards.body: Pentecostalism spread across the nation and the world from the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles, begun in 1906. It was led by William J. Seymour, an African American minister who welcomed worshipers of every race. Pentecostals emphasize baptism with the Holy Spirit, usually shown by speaking in tongues, as at the Pentecost described in Acts.

title: Faith in Black America
objective: After this level you can explain why independent Black churches and Black Muslim movements became pillars of Black American life.
summary: After a 1787 walkout, Richard Allen led the AME Church, organized in 1816, and Black churches became community hubs. The Nation of Islam, founded in 1930, later moved toward orthodox Islam.

cards.headline: In 1787, Black worshippers walked out of a Philadelphia church.
cards.body: What they built next became a pillar of Black American life. This level follows it, and a second movement that began in Detroit.

cards.headline: A church of their own
cards.body: In 1787 Black worshippers left St. George's Methodist Episcopal Church in Philadelphia over restrictions on where they could sit. Richard Allen, formerly enslaved, became their leader. In 1816 he was consecrated bishop of the newly organized African Methodist Episcopal Church, the first African American denomination organized in the United States.

cards.headline: More than Sunday
cards.body: Churches founded by free African American Christians became the hub of Black economic, social and intellectual life in many places. They opened doors for women, if slowly. Allen first told Jarena Lee that the church's rules did not call for women preachers; in 1819 he authorized her to preach, the first woman licensed by the AME Church.

cards.headline: Islam in Black America
cards.body: In 1930 Wallace D. Fard founded the Nation of Islam in Detroit. Under Elijah Muhammad, its leader from 1934, it preached racial unity, self-help and Black-owned businesses, and members often took an X in place of surnames lost in slavery. After Elijah Muhammad died in 1975, his son Warith Deen Mohammed moved followers toward orthodox Islam, and most joined the wider Muslim community.

title: A Nation of Many Faiths
objective: After this level you can explain how immigration since 1965 widened American religion, and what surveys show about Americans' faith today.
summary: The 1965 Immigration and Nationality Act opened America to new Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist and Sikh communities. In 2023 to 2024 about 62% of US adults were Christian, 29% unaffiliated, 7% other.

cards.headline: In 1965 a law changed who could move to America, and how America prays.
cards.body: Today mosques, temples and gurdwaras stand in nearly every major American city. Here's how that happened, and what Americans say about their faith now.

cards.headline: Opening the door
cards.body: The Immigration and Nationality Act, signed on October 3, 1965, ended America's long policy of limiting immigration by national origin, opening new doors for immigrants from Asia. Muslims, Buddhists, Hindus, Sikhs, Jains and Zoroastrians arrived, along with new communities of Jews and Catholics. Now mosques, temples and gurdwaras stand in virtually every major city.

cards.headline: New faiths, familiar ones too
cards.body: Newcomers didn't only bring new faiths. Christians remained most legal immigrants: 68% in 1992 and 61% in 2012. Over those same years, the share belonging to religious minorities rose from about one in five to one in four.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the decimals. Six in ten Christian, three in ten unaffiliated, the rest other faiths.

cards.headline: America today
cards.body: Pew's 2023 to 2024 Religious Landscape Study surveyed 36,908 adults. About 62% identified as Christian, 29% as religiously unaffiliated and 7% with other religions, among them Jews, Muslims, Buddhists and Hindus. After years of decline, the Christian share shows signs of leveling off. And belief runs wider than belonging: 83% said they believe in God or a universal spirit.

title: Religious Law and State Law
objective: After this level you can compare how Jewish law, church law and sharia work, and how religious law has shaped or sits beside the laws of modern states.
summary: Halakhah, canon law and sharia are three great systems of religious law. Each is worked out by scholars, binds believers, and sits beside the laws of modern states rather than replacing them.

cards.headline: Who writes the law when believers say the lawgiver is God?
cards.body: Many faiths guide daily life with law, not only belief. Meet three great systems of religious law, see how scholars work each one out, and find where each meets the laws of a modern state.

cards.headline: Halakhah: the Way
cards.body: Jewish law is called halakhah, Hebrew for "the Way". It reaches well beyond courtrooms, into religious observance and daily conduct, such as keeping the Sabbath. Jews trace it to the revelation at Sinai; it grew through the Mishnah, compiled in the early 3rd century CE, and then the Talmud. Today Jews read it differently: Orthodox and Conservative Judaism treat it as binding, with Conservative rabbis adapting some laws, while Reform Judaism holds most of it not binding.

cards.headline: Canon law: a church's own rulebook
cards.body: Canon law is law made by church authority to govern a church and its members. The Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches all have it. Notice whom it binds: canon 11 of the Catholic Code of Canon Law says purely church laws bind those baptized in or received into the Catholic Church. The state isn't bound at all, though canon law left its mark on secular law, from marriage law to criminal procedure.

cards.headline: Sharia is the path; fiqh is the map-making
cards.body: For Muslims, sharia is a divinely ordained path of conduct, covering their relationship with God, like prayer and fasting, as well as dealings with neighbors and the state. Scholars derive it from the Quran and the Sunnah, the Prophet's example, adding consensus and analogy. That human work is called fiqh, "understanding". Because it is human work, the schools of law hold a wide range of positions on almost every point.

cards.headline: Religious law beside the state
cards.body: So where does religious law meet a modern government? From the 19th century, most Muslim countries adopted Western-style criminal codes and kept sharia mainly for family law: marriage, divorce and inheritance. Put that next to canon law, which binds church members but not the state, and a pattern appears: the believer's law and the state's law run side by side.

title: Why Holy Days Move
objective: After this level you can explain lunar, solar and lunisolar calendars, and use them to predict why Ramadan, Passover, Easter and Diwali move.
summary: Ramadan drifts through the seasons because the Islamic calendar is purely lunar; Passover and Diwali stay in season because Hebrew and Hindu calendars add leap months; Easter follows a full-moon rule.

cards.headline: Why does Ramadan start about 11 days earlier every year?
cards.body: Your birthday sits still on the calendar. Ramadan, Passover, Easter and Diwali all wander. The reason is up in the sky: each festival keeps a different clock.

cards.headline: Three ways to keep time
cards.body: A solar calendar, like the one on your phone, follows the Sun, about 365 days a year, so the seasons stay put. A lunar calendar counts moons instead: twelve lunar months make about 354 days, roughly 11 days short. A lunisolar calendar counts moons too, but slips in an extra month now and then to catch up with the Sun.

mascot.line: Don't memorize dates. Ask which clock a festival keeps: the Moon alone, the Moon plus leap months, or a rule.

cards.headline: Ramadan: a pure moon clock
cards.body: The Islamic calendar is purely lunar: 12 months, 354 or 355 days, and no leap months. So Ramadan, its ninth month, arrives about 11 days earlier each year, and the months slide backward through every season, a full lap in about 32.5 years. Fast through long summer days as a teenager, and half a lap later you'll be fasting in winter.

cards.headline: Passover and Diwali: moon months that catch up
cards.body: The Hebrew calendar is lunisolar. Seven times in every 19 years it adds a leap month, First Adar, so the major festivals stay in season. That keeps Passover, which begins on the 15th of Nisan, in spring. Hindu calendars also add extra months, yet most Hindu festivals still shift against the Gregorian calendar: Diwali centers on the new moon around the start of the lunar month Karttika, in late October or November.

cards.headline: Easter: a rule, not a date
cards.body: Easter follows a rule. It falls on the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox, which the Church fixes at March 21. So Easter can land anywhere from March 22 to April 25: a solar anchor, a lunar trigger and a Sunday, all in one.

title: Food Rules Across Faiths
objective: After this level you can compare kosher, halal, Hindu, Jain and Buddhist food rules and the reasons each tradition gives for them.
summary: Kosher and halal rules rest on scripture and God's command; Hindu, Jain and Buddhist food customs grow from ahimsa, not harming living beings, practiced with very different strictness.

cards.headline: Why would a faith care what's on your plate?
cards.body: Kosher, halal, vegetarian, no onions: food rules are among religion's most visible habits. Line them up and two very different kinds of reason appear.

cards.headline: Kosher: because God commanded it
cards.body: Jewish dietary law permits mammals that chew the cud and have cloven hooves, and fish with both fins and scales. So no pork and no shellfish. Meat and dairy are kept strictly apart. The rules come from the Torah, in books such as Leviticus and Deuteronomy. And the reason? For observant Jews, Britannica notes, no motive is needed beyond God's command.

cards.headline: Halal: the permitted
cards.body: Halal means what Islamic law permits, and haram what it forbids. Pork, alcohol, blood and animals found dead are prohibited, and the slaughterer invokes God's name. Whether a food is halal is judged from the Quran and the Hadith, with analogy and scholarly consensus: the same sources as the rest of Islamic law. Two faiths, one logic: the rule comes from revelation.

cards.headline: Hindu and Jain tables: harm less
cards.body: India's traditions give a second reason: do no harm. Taught by Jains and Buddhists, that ideal was taken up in Hinduism and applied especially to the cow. In a Pew survey of India published in 2021, 44% of Hindus said they were vegetarian. Jains go furthest: 92% said so, and 67% avoid root vegetables, because pulling up roots destroys the whole plant.

cards.headline: The Buddhist alms bowl
cards.body: Buddhism's first precept is to refrain from taking life, yet practice varies. Early monks and nuns ate the alms they were given, refusing only animals slaughtered specifically for them. Vegetarian meals became the norm in Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese monasteries, while in Theravada and Tibetan Buddhism vegetarianism is a personal choice.

title: Why Some Faiths Avoid Images
objective: After this level you can explain why Judaism and Islam avoid images of God, and why Christians once fought over icons.
summary: Judaism and Islam avoid images of God, from the Second Commandment and the belief that God alone gives life. Byzantine Christians fought over icons for over a century before restoring them in 843.

cards.headline: Why would a faith refuse to picture the God it worships?
cards.body: Walk into a mosque and you'll find pattern and light, but no image of God. The reasons run deep, and among Christians they once divided an empire.

cards.headline: "Thou shalt not make"
cards.body: In the King James Version, Exodus 20:4 reads: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above." Its target, Britannica explains, was idol worship rather than art itself. Jewish art never vanished: the 3rd-century synagogue at Dura-Europos was painted with biblical scenes. What stayed off limits was an image to worship.

cards.headline: Islam: God alone gives life
cards.body: Muslims generally reject images of God and of the Prophet Muhammad, seeing them as a form of idolatry at odds with belief in one God. Behind the wider caution about picturing living beings lies the belief that God alone is the author of life, so a likeness can seem to rival him. In mosques, ornament took over: the endless arabesque is said to represent the infinite vastness of God.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: both sides opposed idolatry. They disagreed about whether honoring an icon is worshipping it.

cards.headline: When Christians fought over icons
cards.body: Christians argued too. From the 720s, Byzantine emperors, beginning with Leo III, attacked the veneration of icons as idolatry, citing the Ten Commandments. Defenders replied that images are symbols, that created matter has dignity, and that honor shown to an icon passes to the holy person it shows. After more than a century of struggle, Empress Theodora restored icons for good in 843.

title: Giving as a Duty
objective: After this level you can compare zakat, tzedakah, Christian charity, Buddhist dana and the Sikh langar, and why each faith asks believers to give.
summary: Zakat, tzedakah, Christian charity, Buddhist dana and the Sikh langar make giving a duty, each for its own reason: purification, justice, serving 'the least of these', merit and equality.

cards.headline: Five faiths, one surprising rule: giving isn't optional.
cards.body: In many traditions, giving is a duty, not just a kindness. The interesting part is the reason each faith gives, and how each shapes the gift.

cards.headline: Zakat: a share that purifies
cards.body: Zakat, one of the Five Pillars of Islam, is one-fortieth, about 2.5 percent, of cash and savings above a minimum threshold called the nisab; those below it are exempt. The Quran's ninth sura names who receives it, from the poor and needy to people in debt and travelers in need. The word itself literally means "purification": Muslims believe paying zakat purifies the rest of their wealth.

cards.headline: Tzedakah: justice, not a favor
cards.body: The Hebrew word tzedakah comes from tzedek, justice or righteousness. So giving counts as doing what is right, not optional charity. In his 12th-century code, the Mishneh Torah, Maimonides ranked the ways to give. At the top: a gift, a loan or a business partnership that helps a poor person stand on their own. Just below: giving where neither side knows the other.

cards.headline: "Ye have done it unto me"
cards.body: In Matthew's Gospel, King James Version, a king says, "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat," and "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Buddhists give for another reason. Dana, gift-giving such as food and robes for monks or gifts to temples, builds merit, which Buddhists believe improves karma and leads to a better rebirth.

cards.headline: Langar: everyone eats in one line
cards.body: Sikh gurdwaras keep a langar, a communal kitchen serving vegetarian food to all who come. Everyone sits in a straight line, neither ahead to claim higher status nor behind to show inferiority. It embodies the Sikh principles of selfless service and equality. Five faiths, five reasons: purification, justice, serving "the least of these", merit and equality.
