title: Caste and Its Challengers
objective: After this level you can explain how caste shaped South Asian society and how Buddhists, Sikhs, devotional poets and B. R. Ambedkar challenged it.
summary: Caste ranked people by birth. The Buddha, Ravidas, the Sikh langar, Hindu reformers and B. R. Ambedkar challenged it, and India's 1950 constitution abolished untouchability.

cards.headline: Can a society rank people by birth, and can faith push back?
cards.body: For centuries, caste shaped whom people in South Asia married and what work they did. Here is how it worked, and the religious voices, inside Hinduism and beyond it, that pushed back.

cards.headline: Varna and jati
cards.body: Ancient texts describe four varnas: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras, an arrangement traced to a hymn in the Rigveda. Daily life ran on a finer grid of jatis, birth groups that traditionally married within themselves and were tied to hereditary occupations. People assigned work seen as impure, such as handling dead animals, were treated as untouchable. Many in these communities now prefer the name Dalit.

cards.headline: Not by birth
cards.body: Challenges are old. In a Buddhist discourse, the Buddha teaches that no one is an outcast or a brahman by birth; by deeds one becomes either. The bhakti poet Ravidas, born into a leatherworking caste considered untouchable, sang that all are made from the same clay by the same creator. About 40 of his poems stand in the Sikh scripture.

cards.headline: At the table and in reform
cards.body: Sikhs made the point at mealtime: the langar, Britannica notes, began as a protest against the caste system. Within Hinduism, reformers argued too. The Arya Samaj, founded by Dayananda Sarasvati in 1875, opposed basing caste on birth rather than merit and rejected untouchability entirely.

cards.headline: Ambedkar: a constitution and a new path
cards.body: B. R. Ambedkar, born into a Dalit Mahar family, chaired the committee that drafted India's constitution. It came into force on 26 January 1950: Article 15 bans discrimination based on caste, and Article 17 abolishes untouchability. Ambedkar despaired that untouchability persisted in Hindu doctrine, and in October 1956 he became a Buddhist at a ceremony in Nagpur, joined by a vast crowd of fellow Dalits.

title: Faith and Nonviolent Protest
objective: After this level you can trace nonviolent protest from Jain and Hindu ahimsa through Gandhi to Martin Luther King Jr.'s Christian faith.
summary: Ahimsa, not harming living things, runs from Jain, Hindu and Buddhist ethics through Gandhi's satyagraha to Martin Luther King Jr., whose Christian faith supplied the motive and Gandhi the method.

cards.headline: How did an ancient Indian ideal reach an American Baptist pulpit?
cards.body: Few ideas have traveled as far as "do no harm". Follow it from Jain ethics to Gandhi to a Baptist minister in Montgomery.

cards.headline: Ahimsa: do no harm
cards.body: Ahimsa is the ethical principle of not causing harm to living things, shared by Jainism, Hinduism and Buddhism. Jains hold it highest: it is the standard by which all actions are judged, reaching insects, plants and microbes, and even thoughts. Hindus and Buddhists apply it less strictly. Same ideal, different dials.

cards.headline: Gandhi: holding onto truth
cards.body: Mohandas Gandhi grew up in Gujarat in a home with a strong tinge of Jainism, and embraced ahimsa, vegetarianism and fasting for self-purification. In 1906, facing anti-Asian laws in South Africa's Transvaal, he conceived satyagraha, "holding onto truth": nonviolent resistance to injustice. He drew on ahimsa, on Hindu and biblical texts, and on Tolstoy and Thoreau, and later led campaigns such as the Salt March of 1930.

cards.headline: King: the spirit and the method
cards.body: Martin Luther King Jr., a Baptist minister, first met Gandhi's philosophy as a student at Crozer Theological Seminary. He first put nonviolent direct action to work in the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 to 1956. His own summary: "Christ furnished the spirit and motivation while Gandhi furnished the method." The motive was agape, redeeming good will for all, opponents included.

title: Persecution and the Right to Believe
objective: After this level you can explain how religious persecution, above all the Holocaust, led the world to declare freedom of religion a human right in 1948.
summary: From Roman persecution of Christians to Spain's 1492 expulsion of Jews and the Holocaust, persecution for faith led the UN to declare freedom of religion a human right in 1948.

cards.headline: Why did the world write down a right to believe in 1948?
cards.body: For much of history, holding the wrong faith could cost people their homes or their lives. Here is some of that documented history, and what the nations of the world agreed afterward.

cards.headline: Centuries of persecution
cards.body: Christians suffered persecution in the Roman Empire; the last major wave began under Diocletian in 303 CE, and the Edict of Milan in 313 established toleration. In 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella gave Spain's Jews a choice: baptism or exile. Britannica puts the number expelled at more than 160,000.

cards.headline: The Holocaust
cards.body: The Holocaust was the systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six million European Jews by the Nazi German regime and its allies and collaborators, from 1933 to 1945. After the Second World War, the nations of the new United Nations vowed never again to allow atrocities like those of that war.

cards.headline: Article 18
cards.body: On 10 December 1948, meeting in Paris, the UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with no country voting against. Its preamble names "barbarous acts which have outraged the conscience of mankind." Article 18 answers: "Everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion," including freedom to change religion or belief and to practice it alone or with others, in public or private.

cards.headline: A standard still used
cards.body: The Declaration set a standard that UN experts still hold governments to. In 2022 they said arbitrary arrests of Baha'is in Iran and the destruction or confiscation of their property bore all the signs of a policy of systematic persecution.

title: Religion and Science
objective: After this level you can explain why historians reject the story of an endless war between science and religion, using Galileo, Darwin and Lemaître.
summary: The science-religion 'war' story comes from two 19th-century books. Historians see a more varied past: Galileo the believer, Darwin's mixed readers, a priest behind the Big Bang.

cards.headline: Were science and religion always at war?
cards.body: It's a popular story: brave scientists against a fearful Church. Historians who went back to the sources found something far more interesting.

cards.headline: Where the war story came from
cards.body: The story of permanent war spread through two books: John William Draper's History of the Conflict between Religion and Science (1874) and Andrew Dickson White's A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom (1896). It leans on two episodes, Galileo's trial and Darwin's reception. From the late 1980s, historians such as John Hedley Brooke studied the record in context. Most scholars in the field now see the war model as a shallow and partisan reading.

cards.headline: Galileo, a believer on trial
cards.body: In 1633 the Inquisition sentenced Galileo to life imprisonment for teaching that Earth moves around the Sun. He served it under house arrest until his death in 1642, and was not tortured or executed. Nor did he throw out the Bible. In a 1615 letter he quoted a churchman: the Holy Spirit means to teach how one goes to heaven, not how heaven goes.

cards.headline: Darwin's religious readers
cards.body: Darwin's On the Origin of Species appeared in 1859, and the letters it drew ranged from complete condemnation to active support. The clergyman Charles Kingsley praised it, and Darwin added his words to the second edition. Across the Atlantic, Asa Gray, a botanist and devout Presbyterian, defended natural selection and became one of Darwin's leading supporters.

mascot.line: Two explanations to weigh: a war, or a history too varied for one plot. Galileo, Darwin and Lemaitre are your evidence.

cards.headline: The priest behind the Big Bang
cards.body: Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian ordained a Catholic priest in 1923, proposed in 1927 the theory that grew into the Big Bang. He kept science and faith distinct: in 1958 he called his model a scientific hypothesis entirely outside metaphysics or religion, and he objected when Pope Pius XII suggested in 1951 that cosmology supported creation.

title: Three Kinds of Secular State
objective: After this level you can compare America's separation of church and state, France's laïcité and India's secularism, and weigh what each protects.
summary: The US bars an established church and protects free exercise; France's laïcité keeps religion private; India's secularism gives all religions equal respect.

cards.headline: Three democracies call themselves secular. They mean different things.
cards.body: The United States, France and India each describe themselves as secular. Ask what "secular" protects in each, and you get three different answers.

cards.headline: America: hands off, both ways
cards.body: The First Amendment packs two rules into one sentence: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." Government may not set up a church, and it may not stop you practicing your faith. The rule reaches surprising places. In 1976 the Census Bureau's director said a religion question on the mandatory census would appear to infringe upon the traditional separation of church and state.

cards.headline: France: a neutral public square
cards.body: France's 1905 law says the Republic ensures freedom of conscience, yet neither recognizes, pays for nor subsidizes any religion. This is laïcité: faith belongs to private life, and the public sphere stays secular. So a 2004 law bans public school students from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, from Muslim headscarves and Sikh turbans to Jewish skullcaps and large crosses. Here the state protects a neutral classroom.

mascot.line: Easy to mix up: in India, secular means the state treats every faith evenly, not that it keeps every faith at arm's length.

cards.headline: India: equal respect, not distance
cards.body: India's constitution protected religious freedom and banned religious discrimination from the start, but the word secular joined its preamble only in 1976. Britannica describes a balance between Gandhi's ideal, the equality of all religions, and Nehru's, neutrality toward religion. So the state doesn't simply step back. In family matters such as marriage and inheritance, Muslims may follow Islamic law and Hindus Hindu law.

title: Atheists, Agnostics, Humanists
objective: After this level you can tell atheism, agnosticism and secular humanism apart and explain their long history.
summary: Atheism denies belief in God or spirits and is ancient; agnosticism, Huxley's 1869 word, leaves the question open; humanism is a nonreligious ethical way of life.

cards.headline: Atheist, agnostic, humanist: three labels for three different questions.
cards.body: People often use them as if they meant the same thing. Each one answers something different: what you believe, what you think anyone can know, and how you choose to live.

cards.headline: Atheism: no God, no spirits
cards.body: Britannica defines atheism as the critique and denial of belief in God or spiritual beings; the word comes from the Greek atheos, "godless". The stance is old. In ancient India the Lokayata school, also called Carvaka, rejected god, an immaterial soul and any afterlife, and trusted perception alone as a source of knowledge. None of its own books survive, only fragments.

cards.headline: Agnosticism: I don't know
cards.body: In 1869, at a meeting of London's Metaphysical Society, T. H. Huxley introduced a new word: agnostic. He meant it as the opposite of the "Gnostic" of Church history, who claimed to know so much about things Huxley was ignorant of. That's the difference in one line. An atheist says God doesn't exist; an agnostic leaves the question open, unanswered or unanswerable.

cards.headline: Humanism: a way to live
cards.body: Humanism answers the third question: how to live. Humanists International calls it "a democratic and ethical life stance" affirming that people have the right and responsibility to give meaning and shape to their own lives. Many humanists are atheists and others agnostic, and they don't believe in gods or an afterlife. In 1851 George Holyoake coined another word for this outlook, secularism: a nonreligious ethical philosophy.

title: Is Religion Fading?
objective: After this level you can weigh the secularization thesis against evidence that the world's population is becoming more religious, not less.
summary: Berger predicted religion's decline in 1967, then called the world 'furiously religious' in 1999. Pew data show people leaving religion while religious populations grow.

cards.headline: A top sociologist once saw little future for religion. Then he changed his mind.
cards.body: Is the world becoming less religious as it modernizes? It's one of the biggest questions in the study of religion, and the evidence pulls two ways.

cards.headline: The secularization thesis
cards.body: In The Sacred Canopy (1967), Peter Berger defined secularization as "the process by which sectors of society and culture are removed from the domination of religious institutions and symbols". Think of schools leaving church control. Like many sociologists of his day, the early Berger saw it as an inevitable result of modernization, with little future left for religion.

cards.headline: The about-face
cards.body: About three decades later Berger reversed himself. In 1999 he wrote that "the assumption that we live in a secularized world is false". The world, he said, is "as furiously religious as it ever was".

cards.headline: What the numbers say
cards.body: Pew's count for 2010 to 2020 shows both forces at once. The unaffiliated share rose nearly a point, to 24.2%, mostly through switching: people raised Christian shedding the label. Yet Muslims grew fastest, rising 1.8 points to 25.6%, helped by young populations. The unaffiliated are older and have fewer children than Christians, Muslims and Hindus.

mascot.line: Keep this: 'is religion fading?' has two answers. Many people are leaving it, and the number who belong is still growing.

cards.headline: Weighing it up
cards.body: Both sides have a point. Berger's thesis wasn't simply wrong: most sociologists agree that institutions have separated from religion across much of Europe, and Steve Bruce defended the thesis in a 2011 book. But the number of believers keeps climbing. In that decade Muslims grew by 347 million and Christians by 122 million. People can drift from religion in one place while the religious world keeps growing.

summary: Juergensmeyer shows how religion frames conflict as 'cosmic war' but not as its root cause; Cavanaugh calls 'religious violence' a misleading category.

cards.headline: Does religion cause war? Two leading scholars give different answers.
cards.body: Mark Juergensmeyer studies what religion adds to violence. William Cavanaugh asks whether "religious violence" is even a useful category. Weigh them together, and a better question appears.

cards.headline: Juergensmeyer: a war in the heavens
cards.body: In Terror in the Mind of God, Juergensmeyer studied violence in Christian, Muslim, Jewish, Hindu, Sikh and Buddhist groups, drawing on interviews. His key idea is "cosmic war": not just a fight for religious reasons, but the image of a broader conflict between good and evil, right and wrong. Seen this way, an earthly struggle feels like a battle with eternity at stake.

cards.headline: But not the root cause
cards.body: So is religion the cause? "I don't believe that for a moment," Juergensmeyer said. Violence, in his view, happens for a complex variety of social, political and economic reasons. What religious images and language bring is "a structure of justification and meaning".

cards.headline: Cavanaugh: a slippery category
cards.body: Cavanaugh goes further. In The Myth of Religious Violence (2009) he argues there is no timeless, cross-cultural essence of religion: what counts as religious or secular depends on who holds power. So the idea that religion is uniquely irrational and violent is, he argues, one of the founding myths of Western society.

mascot.line: Watch the word: Cavanaugh's 'myth' is the everyday kind, a belief he thinks is mistaken, not Level 4's sacred story.

cards.headline: Separate the threads
cards.body: Put side by side, the two overlap more than they clash. Neither treats faith as the whole story: Juergensmeyer points to social, political and economic causes, and Cavanaugh to power. So when a conflict is called religious, ask what else is at stake, like land, power or identity. Then ask what the religious language adds.

title: Mystics: One Path or Many?
objective: After this level you can compare Sufi, Kabbalist, Christian and Zen mystics and weigh whether mystical experience is the same everywhere.
summary: Sufis, Kabbalists, Teresa of Ávila and Zen seek the sacred directly. James named four marks of mysticism; Katz argues each tradition shapes the experience.

cards.headline: Four mystics, four faiths. Did they reach the same place?
cards.body: Mystics seek the sacred directly, not only through belief. Scholars have long argued about whether they all find the same thing, or different things in different words.

cards.headline: Four paths inward
cards.body: In Islam, Sufis seek divine love and knowledge through direct personal experience of God. In Judaism, Kabbalah's great book, the Zohar, appeared in medieval Spain and in some circles came to rival the Torah's sanctity. The Spanish nun Teresa of Ávila mapped the soul's journey toward God through prayer in The Interior Castle. And Zen, named for the Sanskrit word for meditation, seeks awakening beyond scripture and words.

cards.headline: James's four marks
cards.body: In 1902 William James proposed a test. A mystical state has four marks: ineffability, a noetic quality, transiency and passivity. The first two are enough. It defies being put into words, yet it feels like knowledge, an insight into truth. You can't describe it, but you're sure you learned something.

cards.headline: Same summit, or different mountains?
cards.body: James heard one voice across Hinduism, Sufism and Christian mysticism, "hardly altered by differences of clime or creed". Perennialists such as Aldous Huxley agreed. Yet James admitted that on a wider view "the supposed unanimity largely disappears". In 1978 Steven Katz went further: there are no pure, unmediated experiences, so a mystic's tradition shapes the experience itself.

title: Cult or New Religion?
objective: After this level you can explain why scholars prefer "new religious movement" to "cult" and how to judge claims about any group by its actions.
summary: Every religion was new once. 'Cult' became a slur that prejudges a group, so scholars say 'new religious movement' and judge each group by what it believes and does.

cards.headline: Call a group a cult, and you've already decided it's dangerous.
cards.body: That's exactly why scholars stopped using the word. Here's the term they use instead, and a fairer test for any group.

cards.headline: Every faith was new once
cards.body: Sociologist Eileen Barker points out that all religions were new at their inception. Early Christianity was a sect within the Judaic tradition; early Methodism was a sect within Christianity. So newness alone tells you nothing about whether a group is good or harmful.

cards.headline: How a word went sour
cards.body: Church, sect, denomination and cult were once technical, non-judgmental terms in sociology. In popular speech today, Barker notes, "cult" can suggest a dangerous pseudo-religion that exploits recruits with brainwashing. Britannica calls "new religious movement" the generally accepted term for what is sometimes called, often pejoratively, a cult.

cards.headline: Definition before discovery
cards.body: Barker's argument is logical. If you want to find out whether a movement commits crimes or abuses its members, you can't build those traits into its definition. So since the 1970s, scholars have preferred "new religious movement". The brainwashing idea, which peaked in the 1970s, has since lost credibility, Britannica notes.

cards.headline: Judge by actions
cards.body: Barker's rule of thumb: don't generalize. New religious movements differ in beliefs, practices, leadership, finances and potential for harm, and no activity is typical of them but not of older religions. So look at what a movement believes and does, at a particular time and place, without confusing the movement, its leaders and its members. In 1988 she founded Inform to give information about minority religions that is as accurate as possible.

title: Interfaith Dialogue
objective: After this level you can describe interfaith milestones from Chicago's 1893 Parliament of the World's Religions onward, and what dialogue does and does not try to do.
summary: Chicago's 1893 Parliament began the modern interfaith movement; Nostra Aetate (1965) rejected nothing true and holy in other faiths; dialogue aims to learn.

cards.headline: In 1893, people of many faiths shared one stage in Chicago.
cards.body: It was the start of something new: religions meeting to understand each other, not to defeat each other. What does that kind of dialogue try to do, and what doesn't it?

cards.headline: The Parliament of 1893
cards.body: From 11 to 27 September 1893, the World's Parliament of Religions met in the building that became the Art Institute of Chicago. It's regarded as the origin of the modern interfaith movement. It was far from balanced: English-speaking Christians gave 152 of the 194 papers, and Native Americans were excluded. In his final address, the Hindu monk Vivekananda said every religion's banner would soon read "Help and not fight".

cards.headline: A church rethinks its neighbors
cards.body: In 1965 the Catholic Church took a step of its own. Its declaration Nostra Aetate says the Church "rejects nothing that is true and holy" in other religions. It regards Muslims with esteem, and it decries hatred and displays of antisemitism against Jews.

cards.headline: What dialogue is, and isn't
cards.body: Dialogue doesn't ask anyone to drop their faith: the same declaration says the Church "ever must proclaim Christ", while urging dialogue and collaboration. Leonard Swidler's ground rules explain the aim: the essential purpose of dialogue is to learn. Each partner describes their own faith. And you compare ideals with ideals and practice with practice, never your ideals with their practice.

title: Myths About World Religions
objective: After this level you can correct common misconceptions, like the idea that most Muslims are Arabs, using what you know about each tradition.
summary: Most Muslims live in the Asia-Pacific region, not the Arab world; Allah is the Arabic word for God; more Christians live in sub-Saharan Africa than in Europe. Many myths treat a faith as one voice.

cards.headline: Most Muslims are Arabs? Christianity is European? Every faith had a founder?
cards.body: All three are common beliefs, and all three are mistaken. Here's the evidence, and a habit for testing any claim about a religion.

cards.headline: Where Muslims live
cards.body: Picture the world's Muslims and many people picture the Arab world. But in 2020, about 59% of the world's Muslims lived in the Asia-Pacific region. Most Muslims, in other words, live outside the Middle East and North Africa.

cards.headline: Not every faith has a founder
cards.body: Many people assume every religion began with one founder. Not so. Hinduism has no single founder, no single scripture and no agreed set of teachings, as Level 41 showed. The Association of Shinto Shrines says Shinto has no founder, no dogma and no doctrine (Level 65). And Jains believe their teachings are eternal: Mahavira is the 24th and last Jina of this age, not their inventor (Level 48).

cards.headline: Christianity's new center
cards.body: Christianity is often pictured as a European faith. But in 2020, 30.7% of the world's Christians lived in sub-Saharan Africa, compared with 22.3% in Europe.

mascot.line: Mind the word: in Level 4, 'myth' meant a sacred story. Here it's the everyday kind, a claim that's simply mistaken.

cards.headline: How to catch a myth
cards.body: Most myths about religion share one habit: they treat a faith as one voice. Remember Smart's point from Level 4: every tradition is a loosely held-together family of subtraditions. And Level 9's lesson: "unaffiliated" doesn't mean unbelieving. So before you trust an "all Muslims" or "all Christians" claim, ask: which ones, where, and who counted?
